arXiv:2602.04022v1 [math.NT] 03 Feb 2026

The Riemann Hypothesis: Past, Present and a Letter Through Time

[Alain Connes]
August 24, 2026
Abstract

This paper, commissioned as a survey of the Riemann Hypothesis, provides a comprehensive overview of 165 years of mathematical approaches to this fundamental problem, while introducing a new perspective that emerged during its preparation. The paper begins with a detailed description of what we know about the Riemann zeta function and its zeros, followed by an extensive survey of mathematical theories developed in pursuit of RH—from classical analytic approaches to modern geometric and physical methods. We also discuss several equivalent formulations of the hypothesis.

Within this survey framework, we present an original contribution in the form of a "Letter to Riemann," using only mathematics available in his time. This letter reveals a method inspired by Riemann’s own approach to the conformal mapping theorem: by extremizing a quadratic form (restriction of Weil’s quadratic form in modern language), we obtain remarkable approximations to the zeros of zeta. Using only primes less than 13, this optimization procedure yields approximations to the first 50 zeros with accuracies ranging from 2.6×10−552.6\times 10^{-55} to 10−310^{-3}. Moreover we prove a general result that these approximating values lie exactly on the critical line ℜ⁡(z)=12\Re(z)=\frac{1}{2}.

Following the letter, we explain the underlying mathematics in modern terms, including the description of a deep connection of the Weil quadratic form with the world of information theory. The final sections develop a geometric perspective using trace formulas, outlining a potential proof strategy based on establishing convergence of zeros from finite to infinite Euler products. While completing the commissioned survey, these new results suggest a promising direction for future research on Riemann’s conjecture.

1 Introduction

The Riemann Hypothesis (RH) stands as perhaps the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics, having resisted all attempts at proof since Bernhard Riemann casually remarked in his 1859 memoir that "sehr wahrscheinlich" (very probably) all nontrivial zeros of his zeta function lie on the critical line ℜ⁡(s)=1/2\Re(s)=1/2.

The essence of this paper is a three pages letter to Riemann, written as if it were possible to communicate across the years, and in which I will present a strategy (towards a proof of RH) which only uses mathematics that he was familiar with, together with the great power of modern computers.

In the section "Encounter with the Riemann zeta function" we aim to convey to the reader a vivid picture of the extraordinary connection that Riemann unveiled between the complex zeros of the zeta function and the distribution of prime numbers. We begin with a short historical account of the prime number theorem, followed by Riemann’s explicit formula for π⁡(x)\pi(x), the number of primes below xx, and its later generalizations into the explicit formulas. From there we turn to one of the most striking consequences: Littlewood’s discovery that the difference π⁡(x)−Li⁡(x)\pi(x)-\mathrm{Li}(x) changes sign infinitely often, an observation that overturned earlier expectations of a simple monotone law.
We then trace the story of what has been established about the zeros of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s), beginning with Hardy’s proof of their infinitude on the critical line, through Selberg’s breakthrough in 1942, and up to modern results concerning the proportion of zeros lying exactly on the critical line. To illuminate this theory, we also draw on the rich framework of entire functions, including Hadamard’s factorization theorem, Nevanlinna theory, and the remarkable Borchsenius–Jessen theorem, itself a success of the Bohr–Landau program on almost periodic functions.
This part culminates with a result that would surely have amazed Riemann : Voronin’s universality theorem. It asserts that the zeta function, in the strip 1/2<ℜ⁡(s)<11/2<\Re(s)<1, has a chameleon-like property: by vertical translation it can approximate any preassigned function f⁡(s)f(s) that is continuous, non-vanishing, and holomorphic on a simply connected compact set within the strip.
Taken together, these milestones show both the depth and the subtlety of the analytic structure of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s). They prepare us to appreciate why the Riemann Hypothesis remains so resistant: the function itself embodies an astonishing range of behaviors, far more elusive than any first impression might suggest.

Riemann could certainly not have foreseen the extraordinary mathematical landscape that emerged from attempts to prove his conjecture. Entire theories were born from this pursuit with connections spanning from algebraic geometry to quantum physics. The section "A century and a Half of Theory Building towards RH" is devoted to a quick panorama of these theories. The first is the extension of the problem into algebraic and arithmetic geometry. In this setting, the analogue of the Riemann zeta function in finite characteristic was developed, and the corresponding analogue of the Riemann Hypothesis was proved by André Weil. To provide context, I will briefly recall the notions of Grothendieck schemes and étale cohomology. The essential point here is that Weil’s celebrated “Rosetta stone” analogy becomes clear when viewed through the lens of schemes. In the original Rosetta stone the parallel inscriptions are horizontal: the hieroglyphs at the top, the Demotic text in the middle, and the Greek at the bottom. Weil proposed a similar three-texts comparison for the Riemann Hypothesis. At the bottom, corresponding to the Greek text, lies Riemann’s work on Riemann surfaces. There is no analogue of the Riemann Hypothesis in this setting, but it illustrates the extraordinary power of transcendental methods in geometry. The middle text corresponds to algebraic geometry over finite fields: here the analogue of the Riemann Hypothesis was established by Weil, with the zeta function arising as the generating function counting rational points on curves over finite field extensions. Finally, the top one, the “hieroglyphic” text, corresponds to the arithmetic case of the spectrum of ℤ\mathbb{Z}, still deeply mysterious.

What is remarkable is that, thanks to Grothendieck’s theory of schemes, one sees a unifying framework across all three inscriptions: in each case one is dealing with regular schemes of dimension one. For this reason, I will briefly evoke schemes, étale cohomology, and motives.

Another major generalization arises from the theory of automorphic forms and representation theory, where the Selberg trace formula and zeta functions play a central role.

I will then move on to random matrix theory and quantum chaos. A remarkable discovery, initiated by Montgomery and Dyson and later spectacularly confirmed by Odlyzko’s large-scale numerical experiments, is that the pair correlation of the normalized spacings between consecutive zeros of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) on the critical line coincides with the correlation of eigenvalues from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE) of random matrix theory. Nicholas Katz and Peter Sarnak extended this correspondence to entire families of L-functions and established a systematic theoretical framework for understanding their statistical behavior as explained in §3.4.4.

In making the comparison of zeta zeros with eigenvalues from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble, one has to rescale locally to compensate for the varying density of zeros. This need for such an adjustment reveals the absence of a genuine “ultraviolet model” for the zeta function—a gap that will be addressed in the final part of this paper, in §7.6.
A further advance came with the work of Keating and Snaith in 2000, who used random matrix theory to propose a conjectural formula for the moments of the Riemann zeta function.

I will then briefly turn to my own work from 1998 on the trace formula. The new ingredient there is that, instead of studying the zeta function directly, one considers the ideal it generates, which is equivalent to focusing on its zeros. Crucially, one can capture this ideal and the associated zeros without defining the function explicitly, nor appealing to its analytic continuation. The key is the construction of a geometric space—the adèle class space—which acquires a central significance as the quotient of the adèles by the ergodic multiplicative action of the rational numbers. This quotient reveals the zeros of LL-functions, not only of the Riemann zeta function, as an absorption spectrum. Recent results underline a precise correspondence between the adèle class space and the class field theory counterpart of the schemes intimately related to Spec​ℤ\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z} that Grothendieck’s theory of the étale site and the étale fundamental group unveiled as a generalization of Galois theory.

The corresponding trace formula is analogous to Selberg’s, but more delicate, since it involves both an infrared and an ultraviolet cutoff. It is precisely here that, for the first time, prolate spheroidal wave functions naturally enter the scene.

I will mention various generalizations of the Riemann zeta function, which broaden the perspective and suggest new avenues of exploration. For completeness, I will also touch upon pp-adic functions: while no analogue of the Riemann Hypothesis is known in these cases, they have nonetheless given rise to a wealth of beautiful developments.

Finally, I will turn in the section "Equivalent Formulations" to the realm of equivalent formulations of the Riemann Hypothesis. The website/book "Equivalences of the Riemann Hypothesis" by Kevin Broughan (2017, Cambridge University Press), systematically catalogs over 100 equivalent formulations. This comprehensive work organizes equivalences by mathematical area:

  • •

    Elementary arithmetic functions

  • •

    Prime counting formulations

  • •

    Analytic equivalences

  • •

    Functional analysis criteria

  • •

    Probabilistic statements

  • •

    Matrix and operator theory

  • •

    Dynamical systems

Some of these equivalents of RH are strikingly simple : for instance, one lets RnR_{n} be the Redheffer matrix, an n×nn\times n (0,1)-matrix with Ri​j=1R_{ij}=1 if j=1j=1 or ii divides jj. Then

R​H⇔det(Rn)=O⁡(n1/2+ϵ),∀ϵ>0RH\iff\det(R_{n})=O(n^{1/2+\epsilon}),\ \ \forall\epsilon>0

These are alluring but treacherous: the history of the subject shows how easily an attempt to solve the problem can be drawn into the gravitational pull of this “black hole” of equivalences.
I will discuss two of these equivalent formulations, first Weil’s positivity criterion, then Robin’s criterion as improved by Lagarias. This latter criterion shows that RH belongs to the type of statements that Hilbert, in his program on the foundations of Mathematics, was hoping to be "provable if true". But Godel’s theorem showed that precisely for this type of statement truth does not imply provability. This will be discussed in details involving Chaitin’s theory of algorithmic complexity.

The next part of this paper, entitled “A Letter to Professor Bernhard Riemann”, is of a completely different nature. It is written in the form of a letter addressed to Riemann himself, in an imaginary dialogue across time. The purpose of the letter is to point out a simple but surprising observation: a strategy towards RH which fits entirely within Riemann’s own mathematical outlook, as exemplified for instance by his proof of the conformal mapping theorem. Importantly, this strategy requires only the mathematical concepts and tools available in 1859.

Concretely, it allows one to recover the first nontrivial zeros of the zeta function by using only a few factors from the Euler product. For example, truncating the Euler product at the prime 1313 and computing with the method described, one obtains an approximation of the first 50 zeros of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) whose precision is best understood by giving the probability that one could get such an approximation by chance. The likelihood that such agreement could occur merely by chance is about 10−123510^{-1235}. To give a sense of scale, this is approximately the probability of correctly guessing the outcomes of over 4000 consecutive coin tosses — a feat so improbable that, for all practical purposes, it excludes both coincidence and computational error.
One might therefore be tempted to conclude: ‘‘This is simply a new algorithm for computing the zeros of the Riemann zeta function.’’ Were that the case, the Riemann Hypothesis itself would follow, since a general theorem ensures that whenever the smallest eigenvalue of the corresponding operator is simple and even11 1 meaning that the associated eigenfunction is even, the resulting approximating numbers form the spectrum of a self-adjoint operator and hence are all real.
This letter to Riemann is followed, in the section The Next Small Steps, by a more detailed discussion of its content, together with an outline of a possible strategy to justify rigorously that, in general, the approximating zeros produced by this method converge to the actual zeros of the Riemann zeta function. While the numerical evidence in support of this is overwhelming, evidence alone is not a proof. In this natural line of attack, a central role is played by the prolate spheroidal wave functions, which I had introduced into this context in 1998.

Computer experiments reveal a striking fact: when expressed in terms of spheroidal wave functions, one obtains an excellent approximation to the function that minimizes the Weil quadratic form. This observation provides strong motivation for the approach. It is of course possible that a complete proof along these lines may encounter serious obstacles. Yet regardless of how far one can progress, this direction naturally opens the way to a deeper exploration, whose starting point is presented in the section Geometric Perspectives — namely, the unexpected relation between two seemingly distant mathematical worlds.
On the one hand, there is the world of the Weil quadratic form. The central fact here is Weil’s remarkable equivalence: the Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to the positivity of certain quadratic forms which involve only finitely many primes. This is striking, since one might expect that addressing the Riemann Hypothesis would require controlling the full infinity of primes. Here, however, the problem reduces locally, to finite collections at a time. Moreover, in this setting, as mentioned earlier, one can exploit the general construction of functions whose zeros lie entirely on the critical line.
On the other hand, there is the world of the prolate wave functions developed by David Slepian and collaborators, with roots in Claude Shannon’s work in communication theory. The key link, established in the seminal work of Slepian, Landau, and Pollak, is a classical second-order differential operator on the line: the prolate operator, obtained as a confluence from the Heun equation—something entirely familiar to Riemann’s mathematical universe. This operator plays a dual role. In the infrared regime, it provides a means of approximating the minimal eigenvector of the Weil quadratic form. At the other extreme, as explained in the final section of this paper, it also supplies a model for a self-adjoint operator whose spectrum reflects the ultraviolet behavior of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function.
Taken together, these observations underline the importance of understanding situations where only finitely many primes are involved, and of clarifying the interplay between the Weil quadratic form and the prolate operator. This connection is established through the trace formula, which I proved in 1998. In the last section, I will reformulate this trace formula using precisely the same ingredients that arise in communication theory and in the work of Slepian and collaborators, thereby making explicit the bridge it provides between the Weil quadratic form and the prolate functions.
Behind the scene there lies a geometric space of fundamental importance: the semilocal adele class space YSY_{S}, associated with a finite set SS of places of ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} that includes the archimedean place. By construction, YSY_{S} is obtained as the quotient

∏v∈Sℚv/Γ,Γ:={±∏pvnv∣nv∈ℤ}\prod_{v\in S}{\mathbb{Q}}_{v}/\Gamma,\ \ \Gamma:=\{\pm\prod p_{v}^{n_{v}}\mid n_{v}\in{\mathbb{Z}}\}

of the finite product of local fields by the diagonal action of the group Γ⊂ℚ∗\Gamma\subset{\mathbb{Q}}^{*} generated by the primes in SS. Weil’s positivity criterion shows that proving the required positivity in this semilocal setting is equivalent to establishing the Riemann Hypothesis (in fact, one also captures the case of LL-functions with Grössencharacters).

A key advantage of this semilocal space, when compared with the full adele class space, is measure-theoretic: here the multiplicative and additive Haar measures are no longer singular with respect to one another, so the quotient behaves well from the viewpoint of measure theory. Topologically, however, the situation is more subtle. For each prime p∈Sp\in S one encounters a periodic orbit of length log⁡p\log p, and these orbits encode precisely the contribution of pp to the explicit formula. Finally in §7.6, I explain the recent discovery in our joint work with H. Moscovici [27], where we show that the eigenvalues of the selfadjoint extension of the prolate spheroidal operator reproduce the ultraviolet behavior of the squares of zeros of the Riemann zeta function and construct an isospectral family of Dirac operators whose spectra have the same ultraviolet behavior as the zeros of zeta.

2 Encounter with the Riemann zeta function

2.1 Classical Analytic Number Theory

2.1.1 Prime Number Theorem (PNT):

In 1852, Pafnuty Chebyshev, proved in [14] that the number π⁡(x)\pi(x) of primes less than xx fulfills

A​xlog⁡(x)<π⁡(x)<6​A5​xlog⁡(x),A≈0.92129A\frac{x}{\log(x)}<\pi(x)<\frac{6A}{5}\frac{x}{\log(x)},\ \ \ A\approx 0.92129

for xx large enough, which allowed him to prove the convergence of the series over the primes pp,

12​log⁡2+13​log⁡3+15​log⁡5+17​log⁡7+…\frac{1}{2\log 2}+\frac{1}{3\log 3}+\frac{1}{5\log 5}+\frac{1}{7\log 7}+\ldots

He introduced two key counting functions ϑ\vartheta and ψ\psi, given as the sums

ϑ⁡(x):=∑p<xlog⁡p,ψ⁡(x):=ϑ⁡(x)+ϑ⁡(x1/2)+ϑ⁡(x1/3)+…\vartheta(x):=\sum_{p<x}\log p,\ \ \psi(x):=\vartheta(x)+\vartheta(x^{1/2})+\vartheta(x^{1/3})+\ldots

proved the identity ∑1xψ⁡(x/n)=log⁡(x!)\sum_{1}^{x}\psi(x/n)=\log(x!) and then used Stirling’s formula. The fact that the asymptotic relation π⁡(x)∼x/log⁡x\pi(x)\sim x/\log x is equivalent to ϑ⁡(x)∼x\vartheta(x)\sim x was surely known to Chebyshev and was part of the math folklore at that time. In fact in their papers [54], [106], both Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin prove ϑ⁡(x)∼x\vartheta(x)\sim x and do not mention explicitly the equivalent result π⁡(x)∼x/log⁡x\pi(x)\sim x/\log x. Their independent proofs crucially established the non-vanishing of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) on the line Re⁡(s)=1\mathrm{Re}(s)=1, using complex analysis techniques including Hadamard’s theory of entire functions. The connection to RH is profound: while PNT requires only that ζ⁡(s)≠0\zeta(s)\neq 0 for ℜ⁡(s)=1\Re(s)=1, the error term π⁡(x)−Li⁡(x)\pi(x)-\operatorname{Li}(x) in the prime counting function is directly controlled by the location of the zeros. Under RH, the error term improves to O⁡(x1/2​log⁡x)O(x^{1/2}\log x). The approximation by the integral logarithm differs substantially from its first term, one has

Li⁡(x)∼xlog⁡x+xlog2⁡x+2​xlog3⁡x+⋯\operatorname{Li}(x)\sim\frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{x}{\log^{2}x}+\frac{2x}{\log^{3}x}+\cdots

The proof of Hadamard that ζ⁡(s)≠0\zeta(s)\neq 0 for ℜ⁡(s)=1\Re(s)=1 contains a beautiful idea that can be understood through the phases of prime powers and reduced to (−1)2=1(-1)^{2}=1. Indeed if for some real number tt one had ζ⁡(1+i​t)=0\zeta(1+it)=0, the complex numbers p−i​tp^{-it} would tend to accumulate at −1-1, using the expansion of −log⁡(1−p−i​t+ϵ)-\log(1-p^{-it+\epsilon}). But then the complex numbers p−2​i​tp^{-2it} would tend to accumulate at 11, thus creating a pole of the zeta function at 1+2​i​t1+2it which is impossible unless 2​t=02t=0.
The next step in the proof of the PNT by Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin stemmed from their need to extract precise asymptotic information about the distribution of primes from analytic properties of the zeta function. They employed sophisticated techniques from the theory of entire functions and this required detailed estimates of the zeta function’s behavior in various regions of the complex plane. While these methods were mathematically sound and represented brilliant mathematical insights, they obscured the conceptual relationship between the analytic input and the arithmetic output, i.e. the asymptotic formula. Edmund Landau provided the first major conceptual simplification by introducing Tauberian methods to prove the Prime Number Theorem, work that appeared in his influential 1909 "Handbuch der Lehre von der Verteilung der Primzahlen". Landau’s innovation involved recognizing that the connection between analytic properties of the zeta function and arithmetic information about prime distribution could be mediated through a general class of theorems known as Tauberian results. These theorems provide conditions under which asymptotic properties of generating functions translate into asymptotic properties of their coefficient sequences. The progression from Landau’s initial Tauberian approach through the Wiener-Ikehara theorem11endnote: 1 The Wiener-Ikehara theorem states that if A⁡(x)A(x) is a non-negative, monotonically increasing function and f⁡(s)=∫0∞A⁡(x)​e−x​s​𝑑xf(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}A(x)e^{-xs}dx converges for Re⁡(s)>1\operatorname{Re}(s)>1, and if f⁡(s)−c/(s−1)f(s)-c/(s-1) has a continuous extension to Re⁡(s)≥1\operatorname{Re}(s)\geq 1 for some constant c≥0c\geq 0, then limx→∞e−x​A​(x)=c.\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}e^{-x}A(x)=c. This result provided exactly the framework needed to convert information about the zeta function’s non-vanishing on Re⁡(s)=1\operatorname{Re}(s)=1 into precise asymptotic statements about prime-counting functions. The application to the Prime Number Theorem involves expressing the logarithmic derivative of the zeta function as a Mellin transform of the Chebyshev function ψ⁡(x)=∑pk≤xlog⁡p\psi(x)=\sum_{p^{k}\leq x}\log p i.e. the equality −ζ′(s)/ζ(s)=s∫1∞ψ(x)x−(s+1)dx-\zeta^{\prime}(s)/\zeta(s)=s\int_{1}^{\infty}\psi(x)x^{-(s+1)}dx. The non-vanishing of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) on Re⁡(s)=1\operatorname{Re}(s)=1, combined with the known behavior of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) at s=1s=1, ensures that ζ′​(s)/ζ⁡(s)+1/(s−1)\zeta^{\prime}(s)/\zeta(s)+1/(s-1) has the required analytic properties for applying the Wiener-Ikehara theorem. The theorem then directly implies that ψ⁡(x)∼x\psi(x)\sim x, from which the Prime Number Theorem follows through elementary arguments to Newman’s simplified presentation shows how mathematical understanding can deepen through the development of more general and conceptually transparent frameworks.
The 1949 elementary proof of the PNT by Selberg and Erdos showed that complex analysis is not logically necessary for proving the theorem. The Selberg sieve, while developed for his elementary proof of PNT [97], became a fundamental tool in analytic number theory. The Selberg symmetry formula

∑p≤xlog2⁡p+∑p​q≤xlog⁡p​log⁡q=2​x​log⁡x+O⁡(x)\sum_{p\leq x}\log^{2}p+\sum_{pq\leq x}\log p\log q=2x\log x+O(x)

exemplifies his ability to find unexpected simplicities in prime distribution.

2.1.2 Riemann’s formula, von Mangoldt paper

In his fundamental paper22 2 which he sent to Chebyshev [90], Riemann was very careful to define which branch of the integral logarithm he was using and to state the conditional convergence33 3 He was a master of conditional convergence and gave the first rigorous proof that conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to converge to any prescribed value or to diverge entirely. Riemann’s rearrangement theorem emerged from his 1854 habilitation thesis ”Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe”, a work primarily focused on extending the theory of Fourier series to more general classes of functions. Published posthumously in 1867, [91], through Dedekind’s editorial efforts. in his formula for the function f⁡(x)f(x) obtained as the sum of the counting functions π⁡(x1/n)\pi(x^{1/n})

f⁡(x)=Li⁡(x)−∑α(Li⁡(x12+α​i)+Li⁡(x12−α​i))+∫x∞1t2−1​d​tt​log⁡t−log⁡2f(x)=\operatorname{Li}(x)-\sum_{\alpha}\left(\operatorname{Li}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}+\alpha i}\right)+\operatorname{Li}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}-\alpha i}\right)\right)+\int_{x}^{\infty}\frac{1}{t^{2}-1}\frac{dt}{t\log t}-\log 2 (1)

where the 12+α​i\frac{1}{2}+\alpha\ i are the non-trivial zeros of ζ\zeta with positive imaginary part and the order of the terms corresponds to increasing values of ℜ⁡(α)\Re(\alpha).
As I will briefly mention at the beginning of my letter to Riemann, it is unfortunate that the care about the various branches of the integral logarithm has disappeared in some modern treatise such as the classic book of Edwards [44], or in some technical papers, where (1) is written as above while there is no function L​i​(z)Li(z) or L​i​(z)+L​i​(z)¯Li(z)+\overline{Li(z)} for which the general term of the series tends to 00. The problem is with the notation since if one follows Riemann closely one finds that the value he considers depends not just on xρx^{\rho} but upon ρ​log⁡(x)\rho\log(x). In fact in the paper of von Mangoldt [107], he correctly defines the meaning that he gives, not to the function L​i​(z)Li(z) but to the function L​i​(ew)Li\left(e^{w}\right). Here is what he writes:

Setting w=u+i​vw=u+iv where u and v denote real numbers, and again understanding hh as a positive real variable, one only needs to make the following definitions:
1. If v>0v>0 , then

L​i​(ew)=limh→∞∫−h+wwezz​𝑑z+i​πLi\left(e^{w}\right)=\lim_{h\to\infty}\int_{-h+w}^{w}\frac{e^{z}}{z}dz+i\pi

2. If v=0v=0, then

L​i​(ew)=limh→0∫−∞−hezz​𝑑z+∫hwezz​𝑑zLi\left(e^{w}\right)=\lim_{h\to 0}\int_{-\infty}^{-h}\frac{e^{z}}{z}dz+\int_{h}^{w}\frac{e^{z}}{z}dz

3. If v<0v<0 , then

L​i​(ew)=limh→∞∫−h+wwezz​𝑑z−i​πLi\left(e^{w}\right)=\lim_{h\to\infty}\int_{-h+w}^{w}\frac{e^{z}}{z}dz-i\pi

It is easily verified that the function L​i​(ew)Li\left(e^{w}\right) defined in this way indeed possesses the desired properties.

Thus von Mangoldt was fully aware of the defect of the notation L​i​(xρ)Li(x^{\rho}) which unfortunately remained used carelessly, even though most authors are (probably) aware of the problem.
One can test Riemann’s formula, reformulated using the function Ei⁡(ρ​log⁡x)\operatorname{Ei}(\rho\log x) in place of Li⁡(xρ)\operatorname{Li}(x^{\rho}) (see (13)) with the help of the computer and one finds a pretty good agreement by taking the sum over a few thousands zeros of zeta.

2.1.3 Explicit formulas

These relate prime-counting functions to the nontrivial zeros of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s), making precise the influence of the zeros on arithmetic functions. Von Mangoldt [107] rigorously proved Riemann’s original explicit formula as deduced from the simpler equality

ψ⁡(x)=x−∑ρxρρ−log⁡(2​π)−12​log⁡(1−x−2)\psi(x)=x-\sum_{\rho}\frac{x^{\rho}}{\rho}-\log(2\pi)-\frac{1}{2}\log(1-x^{-2})

where ψ⁡(x)=∑pk≤xlog⁡p\psi(x)=\sum_{p^{k}\leq x}\log p is the Chebyshev function, and the sum runs over nontrivial zeros ρ\rho. As in Riemann’s case the ∑ρ\sum_{\rho} is taken as the limit of the partial sums for −T≤ℑ⁡(ρ)≤T-T\leq\Im(\rho)\leq T and fails to be absolutely convergent. The error term is of the order of (log⁡T)2/T(\log T)^{2}/T (see [81] Theorem 12.5).
Guinand [52] and Weil [109] later developed more general explicit formulas connecting test functions and their Fourier transforms to distributions of zeros, providing a harmonic analysis perspective on the relationship between primes and zeros. The usual formulation for the Riemann zeta function involves test functions f:ℝ+∗→ℂf:{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{*}\to\mathbb{C} fulfilling suitable regularity conditions44 4 they are continuous and with continuous derivative except at finitely many points where both f⁡(x)f(x) and f′​(x)f^{\prime}(x) have at most a discontinuity of the first kind, and at which the value of f⁡(x)f(x) and f′​(x)f^{\prime}(x) is defined as the average of the right and left limits. Moreover one assumes that for some δ>0\delta>0 one has f⁡(x)=O⁡(xδ),for​x→0+,f⁡(x)=O⁡(x−1−δ),for​x→+∞.f(x)=O(x^{\delta}),\ \text{for}\ x\to 0+,\ \ f(x)=O(x^{-1-\delta}),\ \text{for}\ x\to+\infty. , and their Mellin transform defined as

f~​(s):=∫0∞f⁡(x)​xs−1​𝑑x\tilde{f}(s):=\int_{0}^{\infty}f(x)x^{s-1}dx (2)

They take the form

∑ρf~​(ρ)=f~​(0)+f~​(1)−∑v𝒲v​(f),\sum_{\rho}\tilde{f}(\rho)=\tilde{f}(0)+\tilde{f}(1)-\sum_{v}{\mathcal{W}}_{v}(f), (3)

where the sum on the left hand side is over all complex zeros ρ\rho of the Riemann zeta function, and is in general only conditionally convergent while the sum on the right hand side runs over all rational places vv of ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. The non-archimedean distributions 𝒲p\mathcal{W}_{p} are defined, using f♯​(x):=x−1​f​(x−1)f^{\sharp}(x):=x^{-1}f(x^{-1}), as

𝒲p​(f):=(log⁡p)​∑m=1∞(f⁡(pm)+f♯​(pm)){\mathcal{W}}_{p}(f):=(\log p)\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\left(f(p^{m})+f^{\sharp}(p^{m})\right) (4)

while the archimedean distribution is given by

𝒲ℝ​(f):=(log⁡4​π+γ)​f​(1)+∫1∞(f⁡(x)+f♯​(x)−2x​f​(1))​d​xx−x−1.{\mathcal{W}}_{\mathbb{R}}(f):=(\log 4\pi+\gamma)f(1)+\int_{1}^{\infty}\left(f(x)+f^{\sharp}(x)-\frac{2}{x}f(1)\right)\frac{dx}{x-x^{-1}}. (5)

2.1.4 Changes of sign of π⁡(x)−Li⁡(x)\pi(x)-\mathrm{Li}(x)

Littlewood’s famous 1914 result [75] that π⁡(x)−Li⁡(x)\pi(x)-\mathrm{Li}(x) changes sign infinitely often (assuming RH) demonstrated that the error term in the PNT exhibits complex oscillatory behavior, challenging the empirical observation that π⁡(x)<Li⁡(x)\pi(x)<\mathrm{Li}(x) for all computed values. The first effective bound for such a sign change was given by Skewes [100], who showed (assuming RH) that a crossing occurs before

B=10101034B=10^{10^{10^{34}}}

This enormous bound has been dramatically improved by Lehman [71], who introduced the key idea of deriving an explicit formula for ue−u/2(π(eu)−Li(eu))ue^{-u/2}\left(\pi\left(e^{u}\right)-\operatorname{Li}\left(e^{u}\right)\right) averaged by a Gaussian kernel. It was further improved by Riele [105] (to approximately 6.69×103706.69\times 10^{370}), Bays and Hudson [2] (to approximately 1.4×103161.4\times 10^{316}), and most recently by Chao and Plymen [15] and Saouter, Demichel and Trudgian[93], [94].

2.1.5 Hardy and Littlewood

Hardy’s 1914 proof [56] that infinitely many zeros lie on the critical line used the functional equation and careful analysis of Z⁡(t)=ei​θ​(t)​ζ​(1/2+i​t)Z(t)=e^{i\theta(t)}\zeta(1/2+it), where θ⁡(t)\theta(t) is chosen to make Z⁡(t)Z(t) real for tt real,

θ⁡(t)=Im⁡(log⁡Γ⁡(14+i​t2))−t2​log​π\theta(t)=\operatorname{Im}\left(\log\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{4}+i\frac{t}{2}\right)\right)-\frac{t}{2}\log\pi

By studying sign changes of Z⁡(t)Z(t), he showed infinitely many zeros exist with ℜ⁡(s)=1/2\Re(s)=1/2.

The Hardy-Littlewood work [57] on conditional results showed that RH implies numerous consequences about prime gaps and other additive problems. Their approach built upon Hardy’s earlier work but incorporated more refined analytical techniques for estimating oscillatory integrals and asymptotic expansions. Their subsequent work involved careful analysis of the approximate functional equation for the zeta function55 5 Siegel’s 1932 paper on Riemann’s notebooks shows that while Hardy and Littlewood had independently rediscovered the principal term of this development in 1920 through their ”approximate functional equation” using similar methods (the saddle-point method), Riemann’s work contained additional insights, which provides an explicit representation for ζ⁡(s)\zeta(\mathrm{s}) that is valid throughout the critical strip. By studying the cancellations and oscillations in this representation, they were able to demonstrate that the number of sign changes in Hardy’s ZZ-function, and hence the number of zeros of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(\mathrm{s}) on the critical line of imaginary part in [0,T][0,T], grows at least linearly with TT. It was still unclear if a positive fraction of the number N⁡(T)N(T) of non-trivial zeros with imaginary part in [0,T][0,T], estimated by Riemann as N⁡(T)∼12​π​T​log⁡TN(T)\sim\frac{1}{2\pi}T\log T, lie on the critical line.

2.1.6 Selberg’s early contributions (1940s–1950s):

The breakthrough that resolved this fundamental question came in 1942 through Atle Selberg’s pioneering work, which introduced the innovative technique of mollification and proved for the first time that a positive proportion of nontrivial zeros lie on the critical line. The essential idea in Selberg’s proof22endnote: 2 Selberg’s mollifier was of the form ∑n≤ξαn​(1−log⁡nlog⁡ξ)ns\sum_{n\leq\xi}\frac{\alpha_{n}\left(1-\frac{\log n}{\log\xi}\right)}{n^{s}} where the αn\alpha_{n} are the Dirichlet series coefficients of 1/ζ⁡(s)1/\sqrt{\zeta(s)} with α1=1\alpha_{1}=1. He needed an average of |ζ⁡(1/2+i​t)|2|\zeta(1/2+it)|^{2} times the fourth power of this mollifier. is to multiply the series for ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) by the square of the partial sums of the series for ζ(s)−1/2\zeta(s)^{-1/2}. Selberg’s achievement was to demonstrate that the number N0​(T)\mathrm{N}_{0}(\mathrm{~T}) of zeros on the critical line satisfies N0​(T)≫T​log⁡T\mathrm{N}_{0}(\mathrm{~T})\gg\mathrm{T}\log\mathrm{T}, which immediately implies that the ratio N0​(T)/N​(T)\mathrm{N}_{0}(\mathrm{~T})/\mathrm{N}(\mathrm{T}) is bounded away from zero, establishing that a positive fraction of all zeros reside on the critical line. Selberg’s work [96, 97] revolutionized the study of the zeta function through several key innovations. His work on the distribution of log⁡|ζ⁡(1/2+i​t)|\log|\zeta(1/2+it)| showed it follows a Gaussian distribution with specific mean and variance, presaging connections to random matrix theory.

2.1.7 Proportion of zeros on the critical line:

As explained above, Hardy’s 1914 theorem [56] was quantified by Selberg (1942) [96] who showed that a positive proportion of zeros have real part 1/21/2. Levinson’s breakthrough in 1974 [73] proved that at least 1/31/3 of the nontrivial zeros lie on the critical line, using mollifier techniques that smooth the zeta function near the critical line. Conrey’s 1989 improvement [34] to 2/52/5 used more sophisticated mollifiers and asymptotic analysis. The 2011 result by Bui, Conrey, and Young [12] achieving 41%41\% employed multiple Dirichlet polynomials and optimization techniques from the theory of extremal functions, representing the current state of the art in this approach. Pratt et al [88] have the current record of 41.7%41.7\% based on Feng’s mollifier [46].

2.1.8 Zero-free regions and zero-density estimates:

Classical zero-free regions, such as the one proved by de la Vallée Poussin [106] showing ζ⁡(s)≠0\zeta(s)\neq 0 for ℜ⁡(s)≥1−c/log⁡(|ℑ⁡(s)|+2)\Re(s)\geq 1-c/\log(|\Im(s)|+2), provide explicit bounds on the distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions. Zero-density estimates, pioneered by Bohr and Landau, bound the number N⁡(σ,T)N(\sigma,T) of zeros with ℜ⁡(s)≥σ\Re(s)\geq\sigma and |ℑ⁡(s)|≤T|\Im(s)|\leq T. The best known results show that N⁡(σ,T)≪Tc⁡(1−σ)N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{c(1-\sigma)} for various values of cc depending on σ\sigma, with improvement

N⁡(σ,T)≪T3​(1−σ)2−σ​(log⁡T)5N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{\frac{3(1-\sigma)}{2-\sigma}}(\log T)^{5}

by Ingham [61]. Montgomery and others provided increasingly sharp bounds as σ→1\sigma\to 1. The Guth-Maynard zero density result [53] is the first improvement in Ingham’s theorem near σ=3/4\sigma=3/4 in 85 years.

2.1.9 The Lindelöf Hypothesis:

The Lindelöf Hypothesis states that |ζ⁡(1/2+i​t)|≪tϵ|\zeta(1/2+it)|\ll t^{\epsilon} for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0. If σ\sigma is real, then μ⁡(σ)\mu(\sigma) is defined to be the infimum of all real numbers α\alpha such that |ζ⁡(σ+i​t)|=O⁡(tα)|\zeta(\sigma+it)|=\mathrm{O}\left(t^{\alpha}\right). One has μ⁡(σ)=0\mu(\sigma)=0 for σ>1\sigma>1, and the functional equation implies that μ⁡(σ)=μ⁡(1−σ)−σ+1/2\mu(\sigma)=\mu(1-\sigma)-\sigma+1/2. The Phragmén-Lindelöf theorem implies that μ\mu is a convex function. The Lindelöf hypothesis states μ⁡(1/2)=0\mu(1/2)=0, which together with the above properties of μ\mu implies that μ⁡(σ)\mu(\sigma) is 0 for σ≥1/2\sigma\geq 1/2 and 1/2−σ1/2-\sigma for σ≤1/2\sigma\leq 1/2. While weaker than RH, it would still have significant applications to moments of LL-functions and subconvexity problems.

2.2 Theory of Entire and Meromorphic Functions

2.2.1 Hadamard factorization theorem

An entire function ff has order σ\sigma if

σ=lim supr→∞log⁡log​M​(r)log⁡r\sigma=\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{\log\log M(r)}{\log r}

where M⁡(r)=max|z|=r⁡|f⁡(z)|M(r)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|. The Hadamard product formula states that an entire function ff of order 1 can be written as

f⁡(z)=eA+B​z​∏ρ(1−zρ)​ez/ρf(z)=e^{A+Bz}\prod_{\rho}\left(1-\frac{z}{\rho}\right)e^{z/\rho}

where the product is over all zeros ρ\rho of ff, and AA, BB are constants. The completed zeta function

ξ(s)=12s(s−1)π−s/2Γ(s/2)ζ(s)\xi(s)=\frac{1}{2}s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s) (6)

is an entire function of order one with the Hadamard product representation66 6 The infinite product is defined here as the limit as T→∞T\to\infty of the product over ρ\rho with |ρ|<T|\rho|<T [55, 5, 72]

ξ⁡(z)=ξ⁡(0)​∏ρ(1−zρ)\xi(z)=\xi(0)\prod_{\rho}\left(1-\frac{z}{\rho}\right)

Riemann considers the function (he was denoting it as ξ⁡(s)\xi(s) but, since Hardy, one uses Ξ⁡(s)\Xi(s))

Ξ⁡(s)=ξ⁡(1/2+i​s)\Xi(s)=\xi(1/2+is) (7)

The functional equation ξ⁡(s)=ξ⁡(1−s)\xi(s)=\xi(1-s) implies Ξ⁡(s)=Ξ⁡(−s)\Xi(s)=\Xi(-s), thus the function Ξ\Xi is even and its zeros come in pairs ±α\pm\alpha. Moreover, Ξ\Xi is entire of order 1, for each pair of zeros ±α\pm\alpha, the exponential factors es/αe^{s/\alpha} and e−s/αe^{-s/\alpha} cancel and the Hadamard factorization of Ξ\Xi takes the particularly simple form

Ξ⁡(s)=Ξ⁡(0)​∏ℜ⁡(α)>0(1−s2α2)\Xi(s)=\Xi(0)\prod_{\Re(\alpha)>0}\left(1-\frac{s^{2}}{\alpha^{2}}\right)

where the product is over zeros with positive real part only. The two product representations are the same77 7 using the identity 1−12+i​s12+i​a=1−sa1−i2​a1-\frac{\frac{1}{2}+is}{\frac{1}{2}+ia}=\frac{1-\frac{s}{a}}{1-\frac{i}{2a}} except for the constant factor and while ξ⁡(0)=12\xi(0)=\frac{1}{2}, one has

Ξ⁡(0)=−ζ⁡(12)​Γ​(54)2​π4∼0.497121\Xi(0)=-\frac{\zeta\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)}{2\sqrt[4]{\pi}}\sim 0.497121

This nuance is at the origin of the only "typo" in Riemann’s formula for the number of primes less than xx, where he used log⁡Ξ⁡(0)\log\Xi(0) in place of log⁡ξ⁡(0)\log\xi(0).

2.2.2 Nevanlinna theory

This value-distribution theory [82, 83, 68] studies the growth and value distribution of meromorphic functions through characteristic functions and deficiency relations. It is worth noting that the Nevanlinna characteristic is closely related to Jensen’s formula. For an analytic function ff with zeros aka_{k} in |z|≤r|z|\leq r, Jensen’s formula asserts that, provided f⁡(0)≠0f(0)\neq 0,

log⁡|f⁡(0)|+∑klog⁡r|ak|=12​π​∫02​πlog⁡|f⁡(r​ei​θ)|​𝑑θ.\log|f(0)|+\sum_{k}\log\frac{r}{|a_{k}|}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|f(re^{i\theta})|\,d\theta.

This relation between the average boundary growth of ff and the distribution of its zeros is precisely what Nevanlinna theory systematizes for meromorphic functions. The characteristic T⁡(r,f)=m⁡(r,f)+N⁡(r,f),r>0,T(r,f)=m(r,f)+N(r,f),r>0, can thus be viewed as a refined version of the quantities appearing in Jensen’s formula, with the counting function N⁡(r,f)N(r,f) recording the poles and the proximity function m⁡(r,f)m(r,f) recording the boundary growth. For the zeta function, one can define the Nevanlinna characteristic T⁡(r,ζ)T(r,\zeta) and study its growth33endnote: 3 For a meromorphic function ff in the complex plane, the Nevanlinna characteristic is defined by T⁡(r,f)=m⁡(r,f)+N⁡(r,f),r>0,T(r,f)=m(r,f)+N(r,f),\hskip 20.00003ptr>0, where m⁡(r,f)=12​π​∫02​πlog+⁡|f⁡(r​ei​θ)|​𝑑θm(r,f)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log^{+}\!\big|f\!\left(re^{i\theta}\right)\big|\,d\theta is the proximity function, and N⁡(r,f)=∫0rn⁡(t,f)−n⁡(0,f)t​𝑑t+n⁡(0,f)​log⁡rN(r,f)=\int_{0}^{r}\frac{n(t,f)-n(0,f)}{t}\,dt+n(0,f)\log r is the integrated counting function of poles, with n⁡(t,f)n(t,f) denoting the number of poles of ff (with multiplicity) in |z|≤t|z|\leq t. For an entire function, N⁡(r,f)=0N(r,f)=0 and hence T⁡(r,f)=m⁡(r,f)T(r,f)=m(r,f). In the case of the Riemann zeta function ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s), which is meromorphic in ℂ\mathbb{C} with a single pole at s=1s=1, one can define T⁡(r,ζ)T(r,\zeta) in the same way. A classical result of Borchsenius and Jessen (1948) shows that T⁡(r,ζ)∼log⁡r2​π​∫−ππlog+⁡|ζ⁡(r​ei​θ)|​𝑑θ(r→∞),T(r,\zeta)\sim\frac{\log r}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\log^{+}\!\big|\zeta\!\left(re^{i\theta}\right)\big|\,d\theta\hskip 20.00003pt(r\to\infty), and, more precisely, they obtained the asymptotic T⁡(r,ζ)∼1π​r​log⁡ras ​r→∞.T(r,\zeta)\sim\frac{1}{\pi}\,r\log r\hskip 10.00002pt\text{as }r\to\infty. Thus the Nevanlinna characteristic of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) grows essentially like r​log⁡rr\log r, which is of the same order as the growth of log⁡M⁡(r,ζ)\log M(r,\zeta), where M⁡(r,ζ)=max|s|=r⁡|ζ⁡(s)|M(r,\zeta)=\max_{|s|=r}|\zeta(s)|.. The theory provides tools like the First and Second Main Theorems that relate the distribution of aa-points (solutions to f⁡(z)=af(z)=a) to the growth of the function. While direct applications to prove RH have not succeeded, Nevanlinna theory offers insights into the exceptional nature of the value 00 for ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) as shown by the Borchsenius-Jessen theorem discussed below, and provides analogies with Picard-type theorems [49]. Recent work has explored connections between Nevanlinna theory and the universality properties of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s).

2.2.3 Average behavior of log⁡|ζ⁡(s)|\log|\zeta(s)| and zeros of ζ⁡(s)−x\zeta(s)-x

The Borchsenius-Jessen theorem [7] provides a striking contrast to RH. While all nontrivial zeros of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) are conjectured to lie on ℜ⁡(s)=1/2\Re(s)=1/2, the zeros of ζ⁡(s)−x\zeta(s)-x for any x≠0x\neq 0 cluster densely near the critical line from the right. Specifically:

  • •

    For x≠0x\neq 0, the equation ζ⁡(s)=x\zeta(s)=x has infinitely many solutions in any strip 1/2<ℜ⁡(s)<σ.1/2<\Re(s)<\sigma.

  • •

    The density of solutions increases without bound as ℜ⁡(s)→1/2+\Re(s)\to 1/2^{+}

  • •

    If Nx​(T)N_{x}(T) counts zeros of ζ⁡(s)−x\zeta(s)-x with ℜ⁡(s)>1/2\Re(s)>1/2 and 0<ℑ⁡(s)<T0<\Im(s)<T, then Nx​(T)/T→∞N_{x}(T)/T\to\infty as T→∞T\to\infty

This phenomenon highlights the exceptional nature of the value x=0x=0 and shows that RH is unstable under perturbations: adding any constant to ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) destroys the alignment of zeros on the critical line. The result connects to the mean value theorems for log⁡ζ⁡(s)\log\zeta(s) in the critical strip and to the ergodic properties of the flow s↦s+i​ts\mapsto s+it on the value distribution of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s). The Borchsenius-Jessen theorem can be viewed as the crowning achievement of the Bohr-Landau program on almost periodic functions and Dirichlet series. Where Bohr and Landau established the general framework for understanding value distribution of Dirichlet series through almost periodicity, Borchsenius and Jessen achieved the definitive result for the Riemann zeta function itself, proving that log⁡ζ⁡(σ+i​t)\log\zeta(\sigma+it) has a continuous limiting distribution44endnote: 4 The theorem states that for fixed σ>1/2\sigma>1/2, the values 1T​∫0Tf⁡(log⁡ζ⁡(σ+i​t))​𝑑t\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}f(\log\zeta(\sigma+it))dt converge as T→∞T\rightarrow\infty for continuous bounded functions f:ℂ→ℂf:\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} The limiting distribution μσ\mu_{\sigma} is a probability measure on ℂ\mathbb{C} such that:
- It has no atoms (continuous distribution)
- Its support is the whole complex plane when 1/2<σ<11/2<\sigma<1.
Moreover in spite of the ambiguity in defining log⁡ζ⁡(σ+i​t)\log\zeta(\sigma+it) in the presence of zeros of zeta, the Borchsenius-Jessen theorem does not assume the Riemann Hypothesis..

2.2.4 Voronin’s Universality Theorem, zeta as a chameleon

This remarkable 1975 theorem [108] states that the Riemann zeta function can approximate any non-vanishing holomorphic function arbitrarily well in the critical strip. Voronin’s original theorem established universality for disks: If 0<r<1/4,f⁡(s)0<r<1/4,f(s) is continuous on |s|≤r|s|\leq r, holomorphic on |s|<r|s|<r with f⁡(s)≠0f(s)\neq 0 on |s|≤r|s|\leq r, and ϵ>0\epsilon>0, then there exists t0t_{0} such that

max|s|≤r⁡|f⁡(s)−ζ⁡(s+34+i​t0)|<ϵ\max_{|s|\leq r}\left|f(s)-\zeta\left(s+\frac{3}{4}+it_{0}\right)\right|<\epsilon

Following Voronin’s pioneering work, it was shown by Reich and Bagchi that if KK is a compact subset of the strip {s:1/2<ℜ⁡(s)<1}\{s:1/2<\Re(s)<1\} with connected complement, ff is continuous on KK and holomorphic in the interior of KK with f⁡(s)≠0f(s)\neq 0 on KK, and ϵ>0\epsilon>0, then there exists t0t_{0} such that

maxs∈K⁡|ζ⁡(s+i​t0)−f⁡(s)|<ϵ\max_{s\in K}|\zeta(s+it_{0})-f(s)|<\epsilon

Moreover, the set of such t0t_{0} has positive lower density. Thus, the Riemann zeta function in the critical strip 12<ℜ⁡(z)<1\frac{1}{2}<\Re(z)<1 behaves like a mathematical chameleon: it can approximate any non-vanishing holomorphic function on compact sets simply by shifting vertically in the complex plane. This result uses, as in the Bohr-Landau almost periodic set-up, the ergodic properties of the Kronecker flow on the infinite dimensional torus which is the compact dual of the discrete group ℚ∗{\mathbb{Q}}^{*} of non-zero rational numbers, but we now discuss the key ingredient which is of a different nature.
As we briefly mentioned above in a footnote, Riemann in his memoir on trigonometric series showed, in his discussion of the Dirichlet kernel, that a conditionally convergent series of real numbers can be given any sum CC after a suitable rearangement of its terms. What is amazing is that it is a generalization of this fact which is at the heart of Voronin’s proof. The key result is the following ([70], Theorem 1.16)

The proof of this result is a testimony of the power of the Hahn-Banach theorem55endnote: 5 Besides the Hahn-Banach theorem one uses the following Lemma (see [70] Lemma 1.15) : Let x1,…,xn∈Hx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\in H and let b1,…,bnb_{1},\ldots,b_{n} be complex numbers with |bj|⩽1,j=1,…,n\left|b_{j}\right|\leqslant 1,j=1,\ldots,n. Then there exist complex numbers a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n} with |aj|=1,j=1,…,n\left|a_{j}\right|=1,j=1,\ldots,n, such that ‖∑j=1naj​xj−∑j=1nbj​xj‖2⩽4​∑j=1n‖xj‖2\left\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{j}x_{j}-\sum_{j=1}^{n}b_{j}x_{j}\right\|^{2}\leqslant 4\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left\|x_{j}\right\|^{2} , using the convex set of sums ∑bm​xm\sum b_{m}x_{m} where |bm|≤1|b_{m}|\leq 1.
Voronin’s theorem has been extended to joint universality for Dirichlet LL-functions and other classes of LL-functions, revealing this as a general phenomenon for functions with Euler products. The essence of the proof is to show that, as elements of a suitable Bergman/Hardy-type space HH, the system {log⁡(1−p−s)}\left\{\log\left(1-p^{-s}\right)\right\} where pp runs through the primes satisfies both conditions of the above theorem. This allows one to approximate the logarithm of the function f⁡(s)f(s) (which makes sense since KK is simply connected).

3 A Century and a Half of Theory Building towards RH

Since Riemann’s 1859 memoir “Über die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse,” the hypothesis he formulated concerning the zeros of the zeta function has inspired some of the most profound developments in mathematics. The pursuit of the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), whether explicitly or as a motivating ideal, has led to the emergence of entire theories and reshaped multiple domains. This section provides an overview of major mathematical frameworks and ideas developed in this ongoing quest.

3.1 Harmonic Analysis and Functional Analysis

3.1.1 Hilbert spaces and spectral theory:

The proof of Voronin’s theorem discussed above shows the power of Hilbert space techniques. Hilbert’s inclusion of RH as his 8th problem (1900) coincided with the development of spectral theory. The Hilbert-Pólya conjecture (1910s) suggests the existence of a self-adjoint operator HH such that the non-trivial solutions of ζ⁡(1/2+i​t)=0\zeta(1/2+it)=0 are the eigenvalues of HH. This would immediately imply RH since eigenvalues of self-adjoint operators are real.

3.1.2 Scattering theory and spectral interpretation:

The scattering approach, developed by Faddeev and Pavlov, interprets the zeros of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) as resonances (poles of the scattering matrix) of a certain quantum mechanical system. The Berry-Keating conjecture [3] suggests connections to classical chaotic Hamiltonian systems whose quantization might yield the desired operator. Specific proposals include H=12​(x​p+p​x)H=\frac{1}{2}(xp+px) (where xx is position and pp is momentum) with appropriate boundary conditions, though rigorous constructions remain elusive. The connection to quantum chaos is reinforced by the statistical properties of the zeros matching those of quantum chaotic systems.

3.2 Algebraic and Arithmetic Geometry

As every mathematician knows, one of the time-honored strategies when faced with a difficult problem is to enlarge its scope: to generalize the question and then examine special cases where essential features can be more clearly discerned. Within this setting, André Weil achieved a decisive breakthrough by resolving the analogue of the hypothesis for global fields of finite characteristic.

3.2.1 Weil’s proof for function fields:

Weil’s 1940s proof of RH for curves over finite fields used intersection theory on the product C×CC\times C of a curve with itself. For a smooth projective curve CC over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, the zeta function

ZC​(t)=exp⁡(∑n=1∞Nnn​tn)Z_{C}(t)=\exp\left(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{N_{n}}{n}t^{n}\right)

where Nn=|C⁡(𝔽qn)|N_{n}=|C(\mathbb{F}_{q^{n}})|, satisfies a functional equation and has the form ZC​(t)=P⁡(t)/((1−t)​(1−q​t))Z_{C}(t)=P(t)/((1-t)(1-qt)) where P⁡(t)P(t) is a polynomial whose roots have absolute value q−1/2q^{-1/2}. This is the analogue of RH. Weil’s proof used the intersection pairing on divisors and the Hodge index theorem, establishing a geometric approach to RH-type problems. The successive simplifications of Weil’s proof by Mattuck-Tate and Grothendieck represent a paradigmatic example of how mathematical understanding evolves through the development of more powerful theoretical frameworks. Weil’s original achievement required technical virtuosity to overcome the absence of key theoretical tools. The subsequent simplifications demonstrated how the availability of general results—the Riemann-Roch theorem for surfaces66endnote: 6 It is of the form ∑02(−1)j​dim​Hj​(X,𝒪⁡(D))=12​D.(D−K)+χ⁡(X)\sum_{0}^{2}(-1)^{j}{\rm dim}\,H^{j}(X,\mathcal{O}(D))=\frac{1}{2}D.(D-K)+\chi(X) (8) where DD is a divisor, 𝒪⁡(D)\mathcal{O}(D) its sheaf of sections, χ⁡(X)\chi(X) is the arithmetic genus and systematic intersection theory—could transform specialized constructions into applications of standard techniques. While the classical Riemann-Roch theorem for surfaces originated with Castelnuovo in the 1890s, the sheaf-theoretic version that enabled the Mattuck-Tate simplification was developed by Serre, and the intersection theory suitable for this setting represents a collaborative effort involving André Weil’s foundational 1946 work, Claude Chevalley’s local theory, Serre’s 1958 algebraic formulation, and subsequent developments that created the modern framework of intersection multiplicities using Tor functors and sheaf cohomology.

3.2.2 Grothendieck’s schemes and étale cohomology:

Grothendieck revolutionized algebraic geometry by introducing schemes and étale cohomology [1], partly motivated by the goal of proving the Weil conjectures in arbitrary dimension. The étale cohomology groups Héti​(X,ℚℓ)H^{i}_{\text{\'{e}t}}(X,\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}) for a variety XX over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} carry an action of the Frobenius morphism, and the zeta function is expressed as

ZX​(t)=∏i=02​dim​XPi​(t)(−1)i+1Z_{X}(t)=\prod_{i=0}^{2{\mbox{dim}}X}P_{i}(t)^{(-1)^{i+1}}

where Pi​(t)=det(1−t​F|Héti​(X,ℚℓ))P_{i}(t)=\det(1-tF|H^{i}_{\text{\'{e}t}}(X,\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})). Deligne’s proof (1974) of the Weil conjectures showed that the eigenvalues of Frobenius on HiH^{i} have absolute value qi/2q^{i/2}, establishing RH for varieties over finite fields.

What is particularly inspiring in the study of the étale site of Spec⁡(ℤ)\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z}) is the striking analogy, due to David Mumford and Barry Mazur, between the role of prime ideals in arithmetic geometry and the role of knots in the three-dimensional sphere. In this perspective, each prime can be viewed as the analogue of a knot, and the intricate way in which primes are intertwined within Spec⁡(ℤ)\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z}) endowed with the étale topology mirrors the way knots can be interlaced in S3S^{3}. This vision opened a new topological imagination for number theory, suggesting that the geometry of primes might be understood through concepts closer to low-dimensional topology than to classical analysis. At the heart of this analogy lies Grothendieck’s far-reaching extension of Galois theory from fields to general schemes, accomplished through the introduction of the étale fundamental group. It provides the natural language to interpret the arithmetic of primes in terms of covering spaces, thereby giving a conceptual framework in which Mazur’s and Mumford’s analogy could take shape and develop [77]. We shall come back to this point briefly in §3.5.2.

3.2.3 Motives

Grothendieck’s vision of motives aims to provide a universal cohomology theory that explains the common patterns in various cohomology theories (de Rham, étale, crystalline, etc.). In this framework, zeta and LL-functions are associated to motives, and their analytic properties (including potential RH) would follow from geometric properties of the motives. The motivic formalism suggests that there should be a cohomological interpretation of the classical RH, viewing Spec⁡(ℤ)\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z}) as an arithmetic curve and seeking an appropriate cohomology theory. While the full theory of mixed motives remains conjectural, special cases like Artin motives and motives of modular forms have been extensively developed.

3.3 Automorphic Forms and Representation Theory

In André Weil’s work, the Riemann Hypothesis is naturally recast within the broader framework of global fields. He proved the analogue of the hypothesis for global fields of finite characteristic, and his book Basic Number Theory (Springer, 1967) illustrates how powerful it is to approach number theory from this unifying perspective. A fundamental insight is that, although global fields themselves are countable and discrete, each admits a natural companion: a locally compact, non-discrete ring that contains the global field as a discrete co-compact subgroup. This companion is the ring of adèles, first introduced in the context of class field theory. The adèle ring provides a rich harmonic-analytic structure, and Weil’s reformulation of the explicit formulas in this setting represents a decisive step toward harnessing that structure as a tool in analytic number theory. Weil’s book Basic Number Theory was the first systematic exposition of the use of adèles and idèles in number theory. It not only unified class field theory but also laid the foundation for later developments in automorphic forms and representation theory to which we now turn.

3.3.1 Langlands Program:

This extension of class field theory to the non-abelian case is a vast web of conjectures, initiated by Langlands in the 1960s, it predicts deep connections between Galois representations and automorphic representations. For LL-functions, it predicts that every motivic LL-function (coming from algebraic geometry) equals an automorphic LL-function (coming from harmonic analysis on adelic groups). The proven functional equation is actually one of the key achievements of the automorphic theory, establishing that automorphic LL-functions have the right analytic structure to even formulate the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. Since automorphic LL-functions are expected to satisfy RH, this would imply RH for all motivic LL-functions. The program has achieved spectacular successes (Wiles’ proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem used the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture, now a theorem) but the general conjectures remain open.

3.3.2 Modular forms and L-functions:

The theory of modular forms provides concrete examples of LL-functions with analytic continuation and functional equations. For a weight kk cusp form f⁡(z)=∑n=1∞an​e2​π​i​n​zf(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_{n}e^{2\pi inz} on Γ0​(N)\Gamma_{0}(N), the associated LL-function

L⁡(s,f)=∑n=1∞annsL(s,f)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{a_{n}}{n^{s}}

satisfies a functional equation relating ss to k−sk-s. The Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture (proved by Deligne) bounds |ap|≤2​p(k−1)/2|a_{p}|\leq 2p^{(k-1)/2}, which is the analogue of RH at the level of Euler factors. These examples clarify the expected shape of general LL-functions and their connection to geometric objects.

3.3.3 Selberg trace formula and zeta functions:

Selberg’s trace formula [98, 59] for discrete groups Γ\Gamma acting on hyperbolic spaces relates spectral data (eigenvalues of the Laplacian) to geometric data (lengths of closed geodesics). For Γ=PSL⁡(2,ℤ)\Gamma=\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{Z}), this yields the Selberg zeta function

ZΓ​(s)=∏p​ primitive∏k=0∞(1−e−(s+k)​l​(p))Z_{\Gamma}(s)=\prod_{p\text{ primitive}}\prod_{k=0}^{\infty}(1-e^{-(s+k)l(p)})

where the product is over primitive closed geodesics pp with length l⁡(p)l(p). This function has zeros at the eigenvalues of the Laplacian, providing a complete spectral interpretation. The analogy with the Riemann zeta function is striking: both have Euler products, functional equations, and their zeros encode important information (eigenvalues vs. prime distribution). The Selberg trace formula for Riemann surfaces of finite area, acquires additional terms which make it look e.g. in the case of X=H/P​S​L​(2,ℤ)X=H/PSL(2,{\mathbb{Z}}) (where HH is the upper half plane with the Poincaré metric) even more similar to the explicit formulas, since the parabolic terms now involve explicitly the sum

2​∑n=1∞Λ⁡(n)n​g​(2​log⁡n)2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n}g(2\log n)

(for a test function gg) to be compared with the Λ⁡(n)\Lambda(n) terms in the explicit formulas

−2∑n=1∞Λ⁡(n)n12g(logn)-2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^{\frac{1}{2}}}g(\log n)

There is however a striking difference which is that these terms occur with a positive sign instead of the negative sign, as discussed in [59] §12. This discussion of the minus sign was extended to the case of the semiclassical limit of Hamiltonian systems in physics in [3].

3.4 Random Matrix Theory and Quantum Chaos

3.4.1 Montgomery’s pair correlation:

In 1973, Hugh Montgomery [79, 80] conjectured a striking statistical property of the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function on the critical line. Letting γ\gamma denote ordinates of zeros ρ=12+i​γ\rho=\tfrac{1}{2}+i\gamma with 0<γ<T0<\gamma<T, he studied the two-point correlation function of the rescaled spacings between zeros. Specifically, he conjectured that for 0<a<b0<a<b, and N⁡(T)=∑0<γ≤T1N(T)=\sum_{0<\gamma\leq T}1,

limT→∞1N⁡(T)#{(γ,γ’):0<γ,γ’<T,2​π​alog⁡T≤|γ−γ’|≤2​π​blog⁡T}=∫ab(1−(sin​π​uπ​u)2)du,\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{N(T)}\#\left\{(\gamma,\gamma\textquoteright):0<\gamma,\gamma\textquoteright<T,\;\frac{2\pi a}{\log T}\leq|\gamma-\gamma\textquoteright|\leq\frac{2\pi b}{\log T}\right\}=\int_{a}^{b}\left(1-\left(\frac{{{\rm sin}}\pi u}{\pi u}\right)^{2}\right)du,

This conjectured density reflects a repulsion between zeros and suggests they are not randomly distributed but exhibit a regularity akin to that of eigenvalues of large random Hermitian matrices. In a widely recounted anecdote, Montgomery mentioned his formula during a visit to the Institute for Advanced Study, where the physicist Freeman Dyson, upon seeing it, immediately recognized it as the pair correlation function for eigenvalues in the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE) of random matrix theory. This was verified numerically by Odlyzko to extraordinary precision. The connection suggests that the zeros behave like eigenvalues of a random Hermitian matrix, pointing to an underlying chaotic quantum system. This serendipitous encounter laid the groundwork for a deep and fruitful connection between number theory and quantum statistical mechanics.

3.4.2 Odlyzko’s statistics:

Andrew Odlyzko’s computations in the 1980s-1990s revolutionized our understanding of the statistical properties of zeta zeros. Computing millions of zeros at very large heights (around the 102010^{20}-th zero), he found:

  • •

    Nearest-neighbor spacings follow the GUE distribution with extraordinary accuracy

  • •

    Higher correlation functions also match random matrix predictions

  • •

    Local statistics are universal, but global statistics show number-theoretic fluctuations

His data provided compelling evidence for the GUE hypothesis and inspired much of the subsequent work connecting number theory to random matrix theory. The agreement extends to fine details like the variance of the number of zeros in intervals and the distribution of the arguments of ζ⁡(1/2+i​t)\zeta(1/2+it).

To compare the statistical properties of Riemann zeta zeros with eigenvalues of random matrices from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE), one must address a fundamental incompatibility in their densities. The eigenvalues of an N×NN\times N GUE matrix have constant mean spacing π/N\pi/\sqrt{N} along the real axis (after appropriate normalization). In contrast, the zeros ρn=1/2+i​γn\rho_{n}=1/2+i\gamma_{n} of the Riemann zeta function have imaginary parts γn\gamma_{n} whose density increases logarithmically: the number of zeros with 0<γ<T0<\gamma<T is approximately T2​π​log⁡T2​π\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}, giving a local mean spacing near height TT of approximately 2​πlog⁡(T/2​π)\frac{2\pi}{\log(T/2\pi)}.

To make a meaningful comparison, one must rescale the zeros locally. Specifically, when studying zeros near height TT, one considers the rescaled spacings

γ~n=log⁡(T/2​π)2​π​(γn+1−γn)\tilde{\gamma}_{n}=\frac{\log(T/2\pi)}{2\pi}(\gamma_{n+1}-\gamma_{n})

which have mean value 1. One then compares these rescaled spacings with the eigenvalue spacings of GUE matrices with N∼log⁡T2​πN\sim\log\frac{T}{2\pi}. After this height-dependent rescaling, one finds remarkable agreement in local statistics such as nearest-neighbor spacing distributions and nn-point correlation functions. However, this rescaling procedure highlights that any correspondence between zeta zeros and random matrix eigenvalues must be inherently local and cannot arise from a simple, fixed spectral operator.

3.4.3 Quantum chaos:

The field of quantum chaos studies the quantum mechanics of classically chaotic systems. The Berry-Tabor conjecture states that quantum systems with integrable classical limits have Poisson statistics for their eigenvalues, while those with chaotic classical limits follow random matrix statistics (GUE for time-reversal invariant systems). The appearance of GUE statistics for zeta zeros suggests they arise from quantizing a chaotic classical system [3]. Specific proposals include billiards in certain domains or more abstract dynamical systems.

3.4.4 Katz-Sarnak theory

Building upon Montgomery’s discovery and Odlyzko’s computational confirmation of the connection between Riemann zeta zeros and random matrix statistics, Nicholas Katz and Peter Sarnak extended this correspondence to entire families of LL-functions and established a systematic theoretical framework for understanding their statistical behavior [64, 65]. Their groundbreaking insight was that different families of LL-functions exhibit universal statistical properties governed by one of the classical matrix groups—unitary U⁡(N)U(N), orthogonal O⁡(N)O(N), or symplectic S​p​(2​N)Sp(2N)—with the specific symmetry type determined by the arithmetic and geometric structure of the family itself [64, 42]. The Katz–Sarnak density conjecture predicts that, as the analytic conductors of LL-functions in a family tend to infinity, the distribution of their normalized low-lying zeros near the critical point s=1/2s=1/2 converges to the scaling limits of eigenvalues clustered near 11 in the corresponding random matrix ensemble [64, 65, 66]. Most remarkably, they proved their conjectures rigorously for families of LL-functions over finite fields by connecting the zeros to Frobenius eigenvalues and applying Deligne’s equidistribution theorem [64, 51, 40, 41], thereby providing the first complete verification of random matrix universality in a number-theoretic context. This work not only unified previously disparate phenomena under a single conceptual framework but also provided powerful new tools for studying classical problems in analytic number theory, from the distribution of primes to the arithmetic of elliptic curves.

3.4.5 Moments and unitary matrices (Keating–Snaith):

The asymptotic behavior of moments of the zeta function is conjectured (see [33]) to be of the form :

1T​∫0T|ζ⁡(1/2+i​t)|2​k​𝑑t∼ck​(log⁡T)k2\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}|\zeta(1/2+it)|^{2k}dt\sim c_{k}(\log T)^{k^{2}}

for some constant ckc_{k}. Hardy and Littlewood proved this when k=1k=1 in 1918 and Ingham proved it in 1926 [62] for k=2k=2, one has c1=1c_{1}=1, and c2=(2​π2)−1c_{2}=\left(2\pi^{2}\right)^{-1}. These are the only values of kk where this conjecture is proven, and there was for a long time not even a conjectural value of ckc_{k} for any other value of kk. Conrey and Ghosh [35] conjectured in 1992 the answer for k=3k=3, and Conrey and Gonek [36] conjectured the answer for k=4k=4 in 1998. These two conjectures are of the form ck=ak​gk/(k2!)c_{k}=a_{k}g_{k}/(k^{2}!) where as explained below aka_{k} is a well understood arithmetic factor, but the constants g3=42g_{3}=42 and g4=24024g_{4}=24024 remained mysterious. In the 1998 Vienna conference on RH, Keating and Snaith [66, 67] announced their breakthrough of using random matrix theory to guess the value of gkg_{k}. The new insight of Keating and Snaith was recognizing that the constant fk=gk/(k2!)f_{k}=g_{k}/(k^{2}!) naturally arises from random matrix theory. The general conjecture then takes the form ck=ak​fkc_{k}=a_{k}f_{k} where

  • •

    fkf_{k} comes from random matrix theory (the kk-th moment of |det(I−U)|2|\det(I-U)|^{2} for UU a random unitary matrix)

  • •

    aka_{k} is an arithmetic factor which captures the arithmetic complexity through an Euler product,

    ak=∏p(1−1p)k2​∑m=0∞(Γ⁡(m+k)m!​Γ​(k))2​p−ma_{k}=\prod_{p}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{k^{2}}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\Gamma(m+k)}{m!\Gamma(k)}\right)^{2}p^{-m}

The random matrix part fkf_{k} can be expressed as:

fk=∏j=0k−1j!(j+k)!⟹gk=(k2)!​fkf_{k}=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\frac{j!}{(j+k)!}\implies g_{k}=(k^{2})!\,f_{k}

This separation reveals a beautiful principle: the “universal” behavior comes from random matrix theory, while the arithmetic specifics of the zeta function are encoded separately in aka_{k}. This opened a new paradigm of using random matrix models to predict number-theoretic results, later extended to other LL-functions and their derivatives [38, 50, 104].

3.5 Noncommutative Geometry

3.5.1 Connes’ trace formula

Connes developed a trace formula in the context of noncommutative geometry88 8 The origin came from a system of quantum statistical mechanics exhibiting phase transitions and having the Riemann zeta function as partition function [8] that recovers Weil’s explicit formula for the zeros of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) and of LL-functions [17, 18]. The key insight is to work with the noncommutative space of adele classes 𝔸/ℚ∗\mathbb{A}/\mathbb{Q}^{*}, where 𝔸\mathbb{A} is the ring of adeles. On this space, there is a natural action of the idele class group GL⁡(𝔸)/ℚ∗≃ℤ^∗×ℝ+∗\operatorname{GL}(\mathbb{A})/\mathbb{Q}^{*}\simeq\hat{\mathbb{Z}}^{*}\times{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{*}. The trace formula relates:

  • •

    Spectral side: contributions from the zeros of LL-functions with Grössencharakter.

  • •

    Geometric side: contributions from places of ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}.

In the beginning the trace formula was stated for general global fields as a conjecture equivalent to the validity of the analogue of RH for all LL-functions with Grössencharakter, but the semilocal form of the trace formula was already proved in [17], and it admits as simple corollaries the global versions allowing for the presence of non-critical zeros [78] (see also [18]). This provides a spectral realization where the zeros appear as an absorption spectrum which accounts for the minus sign in the explicit formulas as compared to the Selberg trace formula.
These approaches aim to geometrize the RH using tools from operator algebras and noncommutative differential geometry. An ergodic quotient such as the adele class space 𝔸K/K×{\mathbb{A}}_{K}/K^{\times} of a number field KK is encoded by the cross product of the algebra of functions on 𝔸K{\mathbb{A}}_{K} by the action of K×K^{\times}. The spectral realizations mentioned above involve the Hochschild homology of the cross product of the Bruhat-Schwartz algebra, while the topology of 𝔸K/K×{\mathbb{A}}_{K}/K^{\times} is encoded by the C∗C^{*}-algebra cross product. A recent result [13] shows that this topological encoding is faithful, non-isomorphic number fields give non-isomorphic C∗C^{*}-algebras.

3.5.2 Knots, primes and class field theory

For the global field K=ℚK={\mathbb{Q}}, the projection of the adele class space

π:Yℚ=ℚ∗\𝔸→ℚ∗\𝔸/ℤ^∗=Xℚ\pi:Y_{\mathbb{Q}}=\mathbb{Q}^{*}\backslash\mathbb{A}\to\mathbb{Q}^{*}\backslash\mathbb{A}/\hat{\mathbb{Z}}^{*}=X_{\mathbb{Q}}

on the sector XℚX_{\mathbb{Q}} corresponding to ζ\zeta displays the class field theory counterpart of the Mazur-Mumford analogy between knots and primes mentioned above. To each prime pp corresponds a periodic orbit Cp⊂XℚC_{p}\subset X_{\mathbb{Q}} of length log⁡p\log p. Let then Frobp∈π1e​t​(Spec⁡(𝔽p)){\rm Frob}_{p}\in\pi_{1}^{et}({\rm Spec\,}({\mathbb{F}}_{p})) be the canonical generator of the etale fundamental group and ℤ(p){\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)} the ring ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} localized at pp. One then has [26],

  1. (i)

    The inverse image π−1​(Cp)⊂Yℚ\pi^{-1}(C_{p})\subset Y_{\mathbb{Q}} of the periodic orbit CpC_{p} is canonically isomorphic to the mapping torus of the multiplication by r∗​{Frobp}r^{*}\left\{{\rm Frob}_{p}\right\} in the abelianized étale fundamental group π1e​t​(Spec​ℤ(p))a​b\pi_{1}^{et}({\rm Spec\,}\,{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)})^{ab}.

  2. (ii)

    The canonical isomorphism in (i)(\rm i) is equivariant for the action of the idele class group.

  3. (iii)

    The monodromy of the periodic CpC_{p} in π−1​(Cp)⊂Yℚ\pi^{-1}(C_{p})\subset Y_{\mathbb{Q}} is equal to the natural map

    r∗:π1e​t​(Spec⁡𝔽p)→π1e​t​(Spec⁡ℤ(p))a​br^{*}:\pi_{1}^{et}\left(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{F}_{p}\right)\rightarrow\pi_{1}^{et}(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})^{ab}

    and determines the linking of the prime pp with all other primes.

This result shows that the adele class space plays the role of a class field theory counterpart of the abelian etale covers involved in Grothendieck theory. Quite remarkably the space XℚX_{\mathbb{Q}} admits a topos theoretic incarnation as the scaling site naturally endowed with a structure sheaf of characteristic one (see [20] and the references there).

3.6 p-adic and Motivic L-functions

3.6.1 p-adic L-functions and Iwasawa theory:

Kubota and Leopoldt constructed pp-adic analogues of the Riemann zeta function, which are pp-adic analytic functions that interpolate special values of the classical zeta function. For each prime pp, the pp-adic zeta function ζp​(s)\zeta_{p}(s) is a pp-adic analytic function on ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} satisfying

ζp​(1−k)=(1−pk−1)​ζ​(1−k)\zeta_{p}(1-k)=(1-p^{k-1})\zeta(1-k)

for positive integers kk. Iwasawa theory studies these functions in towers of cyclotomic extensions, relating them to ideal class groups and units. The Main Conjecture of Iwasawa theory (proved by Mazur-Wiles) connects pp-adic LL-functions to Selmer groups of Galois representations. While there is no direct pp-adic analogue of RH, the growth and zeros of pp-adic LL-functions are intimately connected to deep arithmetic phenomena.

3.6.2 Motivic L-functions and Bloch–Kato conjectures:

These far-reaching conjectures relate special values of LL-functions to arithmetic invariants. For a motive MM with LL-function L⁡(M,s)L(M,s), the conjectures predict that:

  • •

    The order of vanishing of L⁡(M,s)L(M,s) at integer points equals the rank of certain KK-groups or Selmer groups

  • •

    The leading coefficient is related to regulators, periods, and Tamagawa numbers

Special cases include the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture (for elliptic curves) and Beilinson’s conjectures. These place RH in a broader arithmetic context where zeros of LL-functions encode geometric and arithmetic information. The conjectures suggest that RH is part of a vast network of relationships between analysis, algebra, and geometry.

3.7 Computational and Experimental Mathematics

3.7.1 High-precision computations

The numerical verification of RH has a rich history:

  • •

    Riemann (1859): computed the first few zeros

  • •

    Gram (1903): 15 zeros

  • •

    Backlund (1914): 79 zeros

  • •

    Hutchinson (1925): 138 zeros

  • •

    Titchmarsh (1935-1936): 1,041 zeros using the Riemann-Siegel formula

  • •

    Turing (1950): verified 1,104 zeros using the Manchester Mark 1

  • •

    Lehmer (1956): 25,000 zeros using electronic computers

  • •

    Rosser, Yohe, Schoenfeld (1968): 3,500,000 zeros

  • •

    van de Lune, te Riele, Winter (1986): 1,500,000,000 zeros

  • •

    Gourdon and Demichel (2004): first 101310^{13} zeros

  • •

    Platt (2021): verification up to height 3×10123\times 10^{12}, [87].

Modern computations use the Riemann-Siegel formula with sophisticated error bounds and the Turing method for rigorous verification. The 1988 publication of the Odlyzko-Schönhage algorithm was a major methodological breakthrough. These massive computations provide overwhelming evidence for RH while also testing for exceptional phenomena [44, 63].

4 Equivalent Formulations

While the previous sections surveyed theories built in pursuit of the Riemann Hypothesis, there exists a parallel tradition of discovering equivalent formulations of RH itself. These reformulations, ranging from elementary number theory to functional analysis, reveal the hypothesis’s deep connections across mathematics and sometimes suggest new angles of attack. There are so many of these equivalent formulations that there is a whole website which is designed to account for them. The main significance that one can find in all these formulations is that the elementary formulations, for instance, the Robbins criterion or the Lagarias criterion, show that at the logical level RH has a very particular logical status which will be discussed in details below.

4.1 Weil’s Positivity Criterion

RH is equivalent to the positivity of certain distributions constructed from the zeros, connecting to Weil’s approach via the explicit formula. The difficulty of solving the Riemann Hypothesis in the analytic formulation, is often primarily attributed to the infinite number of terms within the Euler product.

ζ⁡(s)=∏p(1−p−s)−1\zeta(s)=\prod_{p}(1-p^{-s})^{-1} (9)

However, contrary to this widespread belief, there exists a property P⁡(n)P(n), involving only the Euler factors for primes smaller than nn, and whose validity for all nn is equivalent to RH. This is derived from Weil’s positivity criterion which involves the quadratic form Q​WQW defined using the Riemann-Weil explicit formulas applied to test functions with support in a compact symmetric interval. After a minor change of notations the Mellin transform becomes the Fourier transform for the group ℝ+∗{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{*} whose Pontjagin dual is identified with the additive group ℝ{\mathbb{R}}, and the explicit formula takes the following form, similar to (4), (5) but with notations adapted to the involutive convolution algebra of the group ℝ+∗{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{*},

f^​(i2)−∑12+i​s∈Zf^​(s)+f^​(−i2)=∑vWv​(f)\displaystyle\widehat{f}\left(\frac{i}{2}\right)-\sum_{\frac{1}{2}+is\in Z}\widehat{f}(s)+\widehat{f}\left(-\frac{i}{2}\right)=\sum_{v}W_{v}(f)
f^​(s):=∫0∞f⁡(x)​x−i​s​d∗​x,d∗​x=d​xx\displaystyle\widehat{f}(s):=\int_{0}^{\infty}f(x)x^{-is}d^{*}x,\hskip 10.00002ptd^{*}x=\frac{dx}{x}

where the local contributions are now given by

Wp(f):=(logp)∑m=1∞p−m/2(f(pm)+f(p−m))W_{p}(f):=(\log p)\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}p^{-m/2}\left(f\left(p^{m}\right)+f\left(p^{-m}\right)\right) (10)

and for the archimedean place

Wℝ​(f):=\displaystyle W_{\mathbb{R}}(f):= (log⁡4​π+γ)​f​(1)\displaystyle(\log 4\pi+\gamma)f(1) (11)
+∫1∞(f(x)+f(x−1)−2x−1/2f(1))x1/2x−x−1d∗x\displaystyle+\int_{1}^{\infty}\left(f(x)+f\left(x^{-1}\right)-2x^{-1/2}f(1)\right)\frac{x^{1/2}}{x-x^{-1}}d^{*}x

The key result of André Weil is the equivalence

R​H⟺∑vWv​(g∗g∗)≤0,∀g,g^​(±i2)=0RH\Longleftrightarrow\sum_{v}W_{v}\left(g*g^{*}\right)\leq 0,\ \forall g,\ \widehat{g}\left(\pm\frac{i}{2}\right)=0

where g∈Cc∞​(ℝ+∗)g\in C_{c}^{\infty}\left(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}\right) is smooth with compact support and g∗​(x):=g¯​(x−1)g^{*}(x):=\bar{g}\left(x^{-1}\right). The key point of this equivalence is that the sum on the right-hand side, when evaluated on a test function gg with compact support, involves only finitely many primes (since WpW_{p} vanishes on functions with support in (p−1,p)\left(p^{-1},p\right) ). Thus, even though the Riemann Hypothesis is concerned with the asymptotic distribution of the primes, the equivalent formulation only involves finitely many primes at a time. In [111] H. Yoshida proved the following result (Theorem 1 in that paper)

The proof is a numerical analysis of the positivity of the Weil functional W∞W_{\infty} restricted to the interval (12,2)\left(\frac{1}{2},2\right), and therefore it does not provide any conceptual reason for this positivity that would have a chance to continue to hold when primes are involved.

4.2 Beurling–Nyman criterion:

This remarkable reformulation (Beurling 1955, Nyman 1950) states that RH is equivalent to the density in L2​(0,1)L^{2}(0,1) of the linear combinations ∑1ncν​ρθν\sum_{1}^{n}c_{\nu}\rho_{\theta_{\nu}}, 0<θν≤10<\theta_{\nu}\leq 1, ∑1ncν​θν=0\sum_{1}^{n}c_{\nu}\theta_{\nu}=0 where

ρθ​(x)={θx}for ​x∈(0,1)\rho_{\theta}(x)=\{\frac{\theta}{x}\}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{for }x\in(0,1)

and {y}\{y\} denotes the fractional part of yy. This transforms RH into a completeness problem in functional analysis. Later work by Báez-Duarte and others has provided quantitative versions, showing that the rate of approximation in this criterion is related to the distribution of zeros off the critical line.

4.3 Li’s criterion

Xian-Jin Li (1997) proved [74] that RH is equivalent to the positivity of the numbers

λn=∑ρ(1−(1−1ρ)n)\lambda_{n}=\sum_{\rho}\left(1-\left(1-\frac{1}{\rho}\right)^{n}\right)

for all n≥1n\geq 1, where the sum runs over all non-trivial zeros ρ\rho of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s).

4.4 Elementary Number-Theoretic Formulations
