In 1913 Grönwall proved in his paper "Some asymptotic expressions in the theory of numbers" that

lim supn→∞σ⁡(n)n​log⁡log​n=eγ,γ=limn→∞(∑k=1n1k−log⁡n)\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\sigma(n)}{n\log\log n}=e^{\gamma},\ \ \gamma=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k}-\log n\right)

where σ⁡(n)\sigma(n) is the sum of divisors function and γ\gamma is the Euler-Mascheroni constant. Building on Gronwall’s foundation, Srinivasa Ramanujan made a crucial connection between the function σ⁡(n)\sigma(n) and the Riemann Hypothesis in his work on highly composite numbers. Ramanujan proved that if the Riemann Hypothesis is true, then the inequality σ⁡(n)/n<eγ​log⁡log⁡n\sigma(n)/n<e^{\gamma}\log\log n holds for all sufficiently large positive integers nn. This represented the first direct link between the truth of the Riemann Hypothesis and bounds on arithmetic functions.

4.4.1 Robin’s Criterion (1984)

Guy Robin proved that RH is equivalent to the inequality

σ⁡(n)<eγ​n​log⁡log⁡n\sigma(n)<e^{\gamma}n\log\log n

for all n>5040n>5040, where σ⁡(n)\sigma(n) is, as above, the sum of divisors function and γ\gamma is the Euler-Mascheroni constant. This remarkable result translates the complex-analytic RH into purely arithmetic terms.

4.4.2 Lagarias’ Criterion (2002)

Jeffrey Lagarias refined Robin’s criterion in the form

R​H⇔σ⁡(n)<Hn+eHn​log⁡Hn,∀n≥1RH\iff\sigma(n)<H_{n}+e^{H_{n}}\log H_{n},\ \ \forall n\geq 1

where Hn=1+1/2+⋯+1/nH_{n}=1+1/2+\cdots+1/n is the nn-th harmonic number. This formulation has the aesthetic advantage of holding for all positive integers.
The reformulation of the Riemann Hypothesis as a universal statement over decidable arithmetic properties places it precisely within the class of statements that Hilbert was hoping to consider as "provable" if true and that Gödel’s incompleteness theorems identify as potentially "true but unprovable" ! Chaitin’s algorithmic information theory results demonstrate that such unprovability becomes increasingly prevalent as statement complexity grows. This connection illuminates fundamental limitations in formal mathematical systems and provides a striking example of how even central problems in number theory intersect with the deepest questions about the nature of mathematical truth and proof. Chaitin’s work reveals that mathematical truth and provability operate in fundamentally different domains from an information-theoretic perspective. Most mathematical truths have high descriptive complexity and contain more information than can be extracted from finite axiom systems through deductive processes. This creates a vast landscape of true statements that remain forever beyond the reach of formal proof, with provable statements representing an infinitesimal fraction of mathematical reality as complexity increases. Estimating the algorithmic complexity of the Lagarias criterion reveals fundamental computational barriers in verifying the Riemann Hypothesis through direct arithmetic checking. The dominant complexity arises from integer factorization requirements for computing the sum of divisors function, placing individual verification instances outside polynomial-time computation for general integers. Harmonic number computation and transcendental function evaluation contribute additional complexities that compound the overall computational costs.

These complexity limitations highlight both the elegance and computational intractability of the Lagarias criterion as a verification approach for the Riemann Hypothesis. While the criterion successfully transforms a deep analytic statement into elementary arithmetic, the computational costs of verification reflect the profound difficulty of the underlying mathematical problem. The analysis demonstrates how computational complexity theory provides essential insights into the practical feasibility of mathematical verification approaches and the fundamental relationship between mathematical truth and computational resources.

5 A Letter to Professor Bernhard Riemann

I was invited to give a talk in Varese, on June 4th of 2025, in the Villa Toeplitz, where the Riemann International School of Mathematics is located. In order to prepare this talk, I did, two days before, a pilgrimage in Selasca, the place where Riemann died on July 20th of 1866.

Given the place where I had to give the talk, I took the following challenge:

What could I tell to Riemann that would surprise him

and that would give him confidence that his hypothesis is true?

So what I am going to write now is a letter to him. I will address to him as "Master". The requisite of course is that it is forbidden to use mathematical notions unknown to him or not easily understandable by him. In fact, I will restrict myself to those which he used in his work. After a preliminary remark, the really new stuff is in the second part of the letter.

To Professor Bernhard Riemann

The beautiful formula that you proved in your paper, namely the formula which allows one to compute the number of prime numbers less than xx in terms of the zeros of the zeta function, has been unfortunately badly written in textbooks thus displaying a profound misunderstanding of the middle term of the formula. You let π′​(x)\pi^{\prime}(x) be the number of primes strictly less than xx with 12\frac{1}{2} added when xx is prime and found for the counting function

f⁡(x):=∑1n​π′​(x1n),f(x):=\sum\frac{1}{n}\pi^{\prime}\left(x^{\frac{1}{n}}\right),

the following formula involving the integral logarithm function Li⁡(x)=∫0xd​tlog⁡t\operatorname{Li}(x)=\int_{0}^{x}\frac{dt}{\log t},

f⁡(x)=Li⁡(x)−∑α(Li⁡(x12+α​i)+Li⁡(x12−α​i))+∫x∞1t2−1​d​tt​log⁡t−log⁡2f(x)=\operatorname{Li}(x)-\sum_{\alpha}\left(\operatorname{Li}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}+\alpha i}\right)+\operatorname{Li}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}-\alpha i}\right)\right)+\int_{x}^{\infty}\frac{1}{t^{2}-1}\frac{dt}{t\log t}-\log 2 (12)

You were very careful at the end of your paper in dealing with multivalued functions, but the mathematical language has evolved and, nowadays, one only uses functions with a definite univalent meaning, while the use of multivalued functions is no longer commonly admitted.
In standard textbooks, for instance the classic book of Edwards77endnote: 7 It is not clear if there is a hidden convention in this book, but the following formula written in section 1.15 ”The term involving the roots ρ\rho” ∫C+tβ−1log⁡t​𝑑t=∫0xβd​ulog⁡u\int_{C^{+}}\frac{t^{\beta-1}}{\log t}dt=\int_{0}^{x^{\beta}}\frac{du}{\log u} (with the comment ”where the second integral is over a path which passes above the singularity at u=1u=1”) equates two terms which cannot be equal since the integral on the left takes different values when one replaces β\beta by β+2​π​i/log⁡(x)\beta+2\pi i/\log(x) while xβx^{\beta} does not change. This implies that Riemann’s formula should be rewritten using instead the function Ei⁡(z)=∫−∞zett​𝑑t\operatorname{Ei}(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{z}\frac{e^{t}}{t}dt which has a branch cut discontinuity in the complex zz plane running from −∞-\infty to 00. The correct form of (12) is f⁡(x)=Li⁡(x)−∑ℑ⁡(ρ)>0(Ei⁡(ρ​log​x)+Ei⁡(ρ¯​log​x))+∫x∞1t2−1​d​tt​log⁡t−log⁡2f(x)=\operatorname{Li}(x)-\sum_{\Im(\rho)>0}\left(\operatorname{Ei}(\rho\log x)+\operatorname{Ei}(\overline{\rho}\log x)\right)+\int_{x}^{\infty}\frac{1}{t^{2}-1}\frac{dt}{t\log t}-\log 2 (13) where the sum is over the zeros of zeta with positive imaginary part. the middle term is written as a sum of the integral logarithm Li\operatorname{Li} function evaluated on xρx^{\rho} where the ρ\rho’s are the non-trivial zeros of ζ\zeta.
Now this is obviously a nonsensical sum because xx to the power ρ\rho does not change if one replaces ρ\rho by ρ+2​π​i​n/log⁡x\rho+2\pi in/\log x, where nn is an arbitrary integer. So the constancy of Li⁡(xρ)\operatorname{Li}(x^{\rho}) on this arithmetic progression implies that there is no possible meaning to the infinite sum because it includes infinitely many repetitions of essentially the same term, since the complex numbers xρx^{\rho} accumulate infinitely at least on the circle of radius x1/2x^{1/2}. In fact, von Mangoldt gave, many years after your paper, a detailed proof of your theorem, and he was more careful, up to some extent, in writing the formula … since instead of dealing with Li\operatorname{Li} he considers a well defined univalent function Ei⁡(z)=Li⁡(exp⁡(z))\operatorname{Ei}(z)=\operatorname{Li}(\exp(z)) of the correct variable zz (rather than exp⁡(z)\exp(z)). He then proves your formula replacing the term ∑Li⁡(xρ)\sum\operatorname{Li}(x^{\rho}) by ∑Ei⁡(ρ​log⁡x)\sum\operatorname{Ei}(\rho\log x).

This being said, it is clear from your formula that you knew what is now called the Guinand-Weil explicit formulas. And the new input in this formula, but that wouldn’t surprise you, is that one considers, instead of the function 1/log⁡u1/\log u which you use, an arbitrary test function ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) applied on the prime powers, and one writes an equality which involves what is nowadays called the Mellin transform99 9 The Mellin transform of ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) is defined as ℳ⁡(ϕ)​(s)=∫0∞us−1​ϕ​(u)​𝑑u\mathcal{M}(\phi)(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}u^{s-1}\phi(u)du of this function ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) evaluated on the non-trivial zeros of the zeta function. One obtains in this way an equality which is not really a generalization of your formula in the sense that yours goes one level of subtlety beyond these classical Guinand-Weil explicit formulas since your test function 1/log⁡u1/\log u is singular at u=1u=1. One thing which is striking in these explicit formulas is that if the test function ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) vanishes outside a finite interval [1,x][1,x], then only finitely many primes are involved in its computation, those less than xx. But this is of course the case for your formula which involves the function equal to ϕ⁡(u)=1/log⁡u\phi(u)=1/\log u in the interval [1,x][1,x] and vanishing outside, so this would not be a surprise to you.

But let me tell you, Master, a fact which I find quite supportive of your hypothesis. The fact is the following. I will devise a process with which, by using only a few primes, I will be able to reach the first non-trivial zeros of your zeta function with remarkable precision. Now what do I mean by involving a few primes? I will take a concrete situation and I will imagine that I do not know what are the primes beyond 13. So I only know 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13. Now at first it seems that in order to get any grasp on the zeros of zeta, it is necessary to involve all primes, because all of them are involved in the Euler product which is defining this function. And so it seems quite unbelievable that by truncating this Euler product, namely by only considering the terms in the Euler product which are involving the primes smaller than 13, one could get any hint on the zeros of the zeta function.

So let me describe the process using only notions that are familiar to you. Out of these primes, 2, 3, etc., up to 13, one fabricates a quadratic form. This quadratic form is similar to the quadratic form you were using when you applied the Dirichlet principle in proving the conformal mapping theorem. It is a quadratic form on the infinite dimensional space of functions ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) of a positive real variable which vanish outside the interval [1,13][1,13]. The value Q⁡(ϕ)Q(\phi) of the quadratic form is obtained by applying the explicit formula to the function ψ⁡(v)=∫ϕ⁡(u)​ϕ​(u​v)​𝑑u/u\psi(v)=\int\phi(u)\phi(uv)du/u. Thus because the function ϕ\phi vanish outside the interval [1,13][1,13], the function ψ\psi vanishes outside the interval [1/13,13][1/13,13] and one does not need to use any other prime power than 2,3,4,5,7,8,9,11,132,3,4,5,7,8,9,11,13 to compute Q⁡(ϕ)Q(\phi). Next, I know how to prove that there is a function η⁡(u)\eta(u) realizing the minimum of the quadratic form Q⁡(ϕ)Q(\phi) while ∫ϕ​(u)2​𝑑u/u=1\int\phi(u)^{2}du/u=1. The proof of existence is entirely similar to the proof given by Hilbert in 1900, in his paper "Über das Dirichletsche Prinzip" for the Dirichlet principle. I then take the Mellin transform of the function η⁡(u)\eta(u). I also know how to prove1010 10 See §6.1 that the zeros of this Mellin transform are on the critical line1111 11 Which is normalized here as the imaginary line. This is proved modulo a condition of uniqueness of the minimum1212 12 The proof uses a generalization of a Theorem of Caratheodory-Fejer on Toeplitz matrices, obtained in 1911, one needs to assume that the lowest eigenvalue of the quadratic form is simple and even.

The amazing fact, which I want to report to you, is that when one computes—with the aid of modern computational machines far beyond what was available in your time—the zeros of the Mellin transform of η⁡(u)\eta(u), say its first 50 zeros, one finds an incredible coincidence with the non-trivial zeros of zeta. For instance, for the first zero, you find out that there are 54 decimal places which agree, and so on and so forth. The number of decimal places which agree decreases slowly, and when you reach the 50-th zero, only few decimal places agree.

I have computed these differences (upper bound of) between the values computed using primes less than 13 and the true values of zeros of zeta which I present herewith:

What this is saying is that we have a firm grasp on your zeros, without at any point involving the infinity of the collection of all primes. And moreover we know a priori that all zeros of the Mellin transform of η⁡(u)\eta(u) are on the critical line.

What we do not know is that, when we increase the upper limit, which was x=13x=13 here, the corresponding set of zeros will converge towards the zeros of zeta. This is something which at this point is not proved. On the other hand, it seems that the abstract reason why your conjecture is true is now within reach since we know that the zeros of the Mellin transforms of the minimal eigenvectors ηx\eta_{x} are purely imaginary, and we expect that the ηx\eta_{x} converge to the function whose Mellin transform is your function Ξ⁡(i​t)\Xi(it). The result would then follow from Hurwitz’s theorem, which implies that all the zeros of the limit of a convergent sequence1313 13 uniformly on compact subsets of holomorphic functions whose zeros are on a fixed line are still on that line.

With respect and admiration,

Alain Connes

6 The strategy and the next small steps

We first explain in §6.1 the general result which provides a wealth of entire functions all of whose zeros are on the real line. The goal then is to try to show that, when the upper bound xx (which was x=13x=13 above) tends to infinity, the minimal eigenvectors ηx\eta_{x} converge in a suitable sense so that their Fourier transforms, for the duality between ℝ+∗{\mathbb{R}}^{*}_{+} and ℝ{\mathbb{R}}, will converge uniformly on compact subsets to the holomorphic function that Riemann had introduced as the Ξ\Xi-function in his paper. In fact we shall follow his footsteps and consider the explicit formula he gave for the function kk whose Fourier transform is Ξ⁡(t)\Xi(t). We shall rewrite in §6.2 this function kk as the image by a summation map ℰ{\mathcal{E}} of a linear combination hh of two Hermite functions h0,h4h_{0},h_{4}. The issue, then, is to show the convergence of the minimal eigenvectors ηx\eta_{x} to the function ℰ⁡(h){\mathcal{E}}(h). In fact, one first needs to recenter ηx\eta_{x} to θx​(u)=ηx​(x1/2​u)\theta_{x}(u)=\eta_{x}(x^{1/2}u) which has its support in [x−1/2,x1/2][x^{-1/2},x^{1/2}]. The plan, in order to achieve this goal, is to break it into several small steps. In the second step, §6.3, one introduces, given λ>1\lambda>1, the prolate spheroidal wave functions which give an adaptation hn,λh_{n,\lambda} of the hermite functions hnh_{n} to functions with support in the interval [−λ,λ]⊂ℝ[-\lambda,\lambda]\subset{\mathbb{R}}. The functions hn,λh_{n,\lambda} are eigenfunctions of a modification of the Hermite operator (16), the prolate wave operator PWλ\operatorname{PW}_{\lambda} of (18), obtained by adding to the Hermite operator 𝐇\mathbf{H} the only multiple of the square of the scaling so that the sum commutes with the orthogonal projection on functions with support in the interval [−λ,λ]⊂ℝ[-\lambda,\lambda]\subset{\mathbb{R}}. By construction PWλ\operatorname{PW}_{\lambda} admits two regular singular points at the boundary ±λ\pm\lambda of the interval and an irregular singularity at ∞\infty. The third step §6.4, consists in making an educated guess for an approximation of the minimal eigenvector θx\theta_{x} by using the same process as in the simple case of §6.2. Thus one simply replaces the Hermite functions h0,h4h_{0},h_{4} by their localizations h0,λ,h4,λh_{0,\lambda},h_{4,\lambda}, for λ=x1/2\lambda=x^{1/2}, and one applies the summation map ℰ{\mathcal{E}} to the linear combination of these two functions with vanishing integral. One obtains in this manner a function kλk_{\lambda} which approximates θx\theta_{x} on the interval [x−1/2,x1/2][x^{-1/2},x^{1/2}]. In §6.5 one shows that, when λ→∞\lambda\to\infty, the Fourier transforms k^λ\widehat{k}_{\lambda} converge towards the Ξ\Xi function of Riemann, uniformly on closed substrips of the open strip of width 11 neighborhood of the real line. Finally in §6.6 we point to the missing final steps.

6.1 The Fourier transform of θx\theta_{x} has all its zeros on the real line

The proof of this result follows from a theorem shown in a joint paper [32] with Walter van Suijlekom, entitled "Quadratic Forms, Real Zeros and Echoes of the Spectral Action". The precise statement is :

Theorem 6.1.

Let L>0L>0, 𝒟\mathcal{D} be a real distribution on the interval [0,L][0,L] and 𝒟~\tilde{\mathcal{D}} the associated even distribution on [−L,L][-L,L]. Assume that the quadratic form with Schwartz kernel 𝒟~​(x−y)\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(x-y) defines a lower-bounded selfadjoint operator on L2​([−L2,L2])L^{2}([-\frac{L}{2},\frac{L}{2}]), and that the minimum of its spectrum is a simple, isolated eigenvalue, with even eigenfunction η\eta. Then all the zeros of the entire function η^​(z)\widehat{\eta}(z), z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}, Fourier transform of η\eta lie on the real line.

The proof of this theorem is based on the special form of the matrix of the quadratic form in the trigonometric orthonormal basis, the construction for finite matrices of that special form of a selfadjoint operator and the above mentioned Hurwitz theorem to pass to the limit when the size of the matrices tends to infinity. The validity of the result on the zeros of the Fourier transform for finite truncations [32] plays a key role in numerical computations1414 14 It is used for the trigonometric truncation at N=100N=100 in the computation presented in the letter and allows one to approximate the zeros of η^​(z)\widehat{\eta}(z) by the spectrum of a rank one perturbation of the periodic Dirac operator, obtained using the Dirichlet kernel analysed by Riemann in [91].

6.3 The prolate wave functions enter the scene

The next step requires introducing a family of functions whose pivotal role in signal transmission was uncovered by Slepian, Pollak, and Landau at Bell Labs during the 1960s. Their work addressed a fundamental question first posed by Claude Shannon in his foundational study on entropy1616 16 C. E. Shannon, Communication in the Presence of Noise, Proc. IRE 37 (1949), 10–21.: To what extent can functions that are band-limited also be time-limited? Shannon had estimated that the number NN of orthogonal signals that can be packed into a time window TT and frequency band WW satisfies N≃2​T​WN\simeq 2TW. Building on this, Slepian and his collaborators sought to maximize the information transmittable over a limited time within a given bandwidth — a problem central to efficient communication systems.

To describe their result, fix the time and frequency interval as [−λ,λ]⊂ℝ[-\lambda,\lambda]\subset\mathbb{R}, and let PλP_{\lambda} be the projection in the Hilbert space L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) (square-integrable functions) defined by multiplication with the characteristic function of the interval [−λ,λ][-\lambda,\lambda]. In their seminal paper, [101], Slepian and Pollak showed that the compressed Fourier transform Pλ​𝔽eℝ​PλP_{\lambda}\mathbb{F}_{e_{\mathbb{R}}}P_{\lambda} commutes with the second-order differential operator

PWλ:=−∂x((λ2−x2)∂x)+(2πλx)2.\operatorname{PW}_{\lambda}:=-\partial_{x}\left((\lambda^{2}-x^{2})\partial_{x}\right)+(2\pi\lambda x)^{2}. (18)

6.6 Remaining steps

In order to apply Theorem 6.1 one needs to show that the smallest eigenvalue of the Weil quadratic form Q​WλQW_{\lambda} is simple with even eigenvector. The analogue of this property is known for the prolate wave operator. Moreover it still remains to show that kλk_{\lambda} is a sufficiently good approximation of θx\theta_{x}, λ=x\lambda=\sqrt{x}.

7 Geometric Perspectives

The geometric approach pursued in the joint work [19] described in [20] unveiled a novel geometric landscape which is a natural analogue, for the global field ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}, of the geometry associated to global fields in finite characteristic. In particular the Frobenius correspondences make sense on the square of the scaling site and the completed Riemann zeta function appears as the analogue of the Hasse-Weil generating function. The handling of the delicate principal values involved in the Riemann-Weil explicit formula required to use the adelic incarnation of the scaling site which we now understand as its class field theory counterpart [26].
In the paper [24], we began to exploit the adelic interpretation of the Frobenius correspondences for the number field ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} in order to gradually investigate Weil’s positivity. As explained in §4.1 the Weil positivity, which only involves finitely many primes at a time, is equivalent to RH. In the adelic geometric framework, the correspondences are encoded by Schwartz kernels, which are distributions in the square of the adelic data that play the role of the class field theory counterpart of the geometric curve. More generally the connection between the operator theoretic and the geometric viewpoints is effected by the Schwartz kernels associated to operators. By implementing the additive structure of the adeles, one sees that the Schwartz kernel of the scaling operator corresponds geometrically to the divisor of the Frobenius correspondence.

7.1 Archimedean trace formula

There is a very important parallel between the Weil quadratic form and the trace formula, on one hand, and the world of information theory. The starting point of this parallel is to rewrite the archimedean case of the trace formula of [17] by involving now two independent parameters which play the role of the time limitation and frequency limitation in the approach of Shannon, Slepian and their collaborators concerning the transmission of information. One works in the Hilbert space L2​(ℝ)evL^{2}(\mathbb{R})_{\mathrm{ev}} of even square integrable functions. The scaling action of ℝ+∗\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*} is defined as

(ϑλξ)(v):=λ−1/2ξ(λ−1v),ϑ(f)=∫f(λ)ϑλd∗λ,∀ξ∈L2(ℝ)ev(\vartheta_{\lambda}\xi)(v):=\lambda^{-1/2}\xi\left(\lambda^{-1}v\right),\ \vartheta(f)=\int f(\lambda)\ \vartheta_{\lambda}d^{*}\lambda,\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\xi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R})_{\mathrm{ev}}

The parameter TT which gives the limitation in time to the interval [−T,T][-T,T] defines the orthogonal projection PTP_{T} and the parameter WW which gives the limitation in frequency to the interval [−W,W][-W,W] defines the projection P^W\widehat{P}_{W}. One can write the archimedean case of the trace formula of [17] as follows, where W∞:=−WℝW_{\infty}:=-W_{\mathbb{R}} was defined in (11):

We view this formula as a bridge between the explicit formulas and the world of information theory where the projections PTP_{T} and P^W\widehat{P}_{W} play a central role. It will be extended below in §7.4 to incorporate the contribution of the primes to the explicit formulas.

7.2 Archimedean Weil positivity

The key ingredient is the semilocal trace formula, which in our paper was used in the simple case when no primes are involved. What we found is that not only Weil’s positivity holds in that case, as explained in §4.1, but the main source of positivity is due to the Sonin space, first introduced in the context of RH by Burnol [9, 10, 11]. The Sonin space 𝔖λ{\mathfrak{S}}_{\lambda} is the space of square integrable functions which vanish identically in the interval [−λ,λ][-\lambda,\lambda] as well as their Fourier transform. It is by construction the orthogonal of the ranges of the projections PλP_{\lambda} and Pλ^\widehat{P_{\lambda}}. We denote by 𝔖{\mathfrak{S}} the orthogonal projection in L2​(ℝ)evL^{2}(\mathbb{R})_{\mathrm{ev}} to the Sonin space 𝔖1{\mathfrak{S}}_{1} (for λ=1\lambda=1). One then has [24],

Theorem 7.1.

Let g∈Cc∞​(ℝ+∗)g\in C_{c}^{\infty}\left(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}\right) have support in the interval [2−1/2,21/2]\left[2^{-1/2},2^{1/2}\right] and Fourier transform vanishing at i2\frac{i}{2} and 0 . Then the following inequality holds

W∞​(g∗g∗)≥Tr⁡(ϑ⁡(g)​𝔖​ϑ​(g)∗)W_{\infty}\left(g*g^{*}\right)\geq\operatorname{Tr}\left(\vartheta(g){\mathfrak{S}}\vartheta(g)^{*}\right)

7.3 The semilocal adele class space

Underlying the semilocal trace formula discussed in §7.4, are the semilocal adele class spaces. These geometric spaces YSY_{S} are associated with a finite set SS of places of ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} containing the infinite place. By construction YSY_{S} is the quotient

YS:=𝔸S/ΓS,𝔸S=∏v∈SℚvY_{S}:={\mathbb{A}}_{S}/\Gamma_{S},\ \ {\mathbb{A}}_{S}=\prod_{v\in S}{\mathbb{Q}}_{v} (23)

of the adelic space product of the local fields completions of the global field ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} at the places v∈Sv\in S. The group ΓS\Gamma_{S} is the subgroup of ℚ×{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times} defined by

ΓS:={±p1n1⋯pknk:pj∈S∖{∞},nj∈ℤ}⊂ℚ×\Gamma_{S}:=\{\pm p_{1}^{n_{1}}\cdots p_{k}^{n_{k}}\,:\,p_{j}\in S\setminus\{\infty\}\,,\,n_{j}\in{\mathbb{Z}}\}\subset{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times} (24)

The ring 𝔸S{\mathbb{A}}_{S} contains ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} as a subring using the diagonal embedding and this induces the action of ΓS\Gamma_{S} on 𝔸S{\mathbb{A}}_{S} by multiplication. The semilocal adele class spaces are best encoded by the noncommutative algebras 𝒮⁡(𝔸S)⋊ΓS{\mathcal{S}}({\mathbb{A}}_{S})\rtimes\Gamma_{S} cross products of the Bruhat-Schwartz algebras 𝒮⁡(𝔸S){\mathcal{S}}({\mathbb{A}}_{S}) of functions on semilocal adeles, by the multiplicative groups ΓS\Gamma_{S}. These noncommutative algebras constitute a sheaf of algebras over Spec​ℤ{\rm Spec\,}\,{\mathbb{Z}}. The group ΓS\Gamma_{S} is properly understood as sections ℤS×{\mathbb{Z}}_{S}^{\times} of the sheaf 𝐆m\mathbf{G}_{m} on the open set complement of SS in Spec​ℤ{\rm Spec\,}\,{\mathbb{Z}}. One shows that the semilocal Bruhat-Schwartz algebra 𝒮⁡(𝔸S){\mathcal{S}}({\mathbb{A}}_{S}) form a sheaf 𝒪{\mathscr{O}} of commutative algebras over Spec​ℤ{\rm Spec\,}\,{\mathbb{Z}}. One then obtains the following result which establishes the compatibility of the noncommutative geometric constructions with the algebraic geometry of Spec​ℤ{\rm Spec\,}\,{\mathbb{Z}}.

Theorem 7.2.
  1. 1.

    The algebraic cross product 𝒪⋊𝐆m{\mathscr{O}}\rtimes\mathbf{G}_{m} defines a sheaf of algebras on Spec​ℤ{\rm Spec\,}{\mathbb{Z}} such that for every finite set of places S∋∞S\ni\infty

    (𝒪⋊𝐆m)​(Sc)=𝒮⁡(𝔸S)⋊ℤS×\left({\mathscr{O}}\rtimes\mathbf{G}_{m}\right)(S^{c})={\mathcal{S}}({\mathbb{A}}_{S})\rtimes{\mathbb{Z}}_{S}^{\times}
  2. 2.

    The stalk of 𝒪⋊𝐆m{\mathscr{O}}\rtimes\mathbf{G}_{m} at the generic point is the global cross product 𝒮⁡(𝔸ℚ)⋊ℚ×{\mathcal{S}}({\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbb{Q}})\rtimes{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times}.

  3. 3.

    The global sections of 𝒪⋊𝐆m{\mathscr{O}}\rtimes\mathbf{G}_{m} form the cross product 𝒮⁡(ℝ)⋊{±1}{\mathcal{S}}({\mathbb{R}})\rtimes\{\pm 1\}.

The function spaces involved in the semilocal trace formula of §7.4 are best understood conceptually as the Hochschild homology of the semilocal algebras.

7.4 The semilocal trace formula

The remaining difficulty in proving that the eigenvectors θx\theta_{x} converge to the function k=ℰ⁡(h)k={\mathcal{E}}(h) of Fact 6.2 is to effectively compare θx\theta_{x} with kλk_{\lambda} for λ=x\lambda=\sqrt{x}. The numerical evidence was shown in [25] where the comparison was extended to the eigenvectors of Q​WλQW_{\lambda} corresponding to the first minuscule eigenvalues, using the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalisation of vectors of the form ℰ⁡(ψ){\mathcal{E}}(\psi) where the ψ\psi are constructed using the next prolate wave functions.
As a step towards a conceptual justification of this numerical fact one has the semilocal trace formula of [17]. It provides a trace formula representation of the Weil quadratic form Q​WλQW_{\lambda} which is perfectly analogous to (22), but now gives the contribution of the primes p∈Sp\in S to the explicit formula. It takes the form

7.5 The infrared and ultraviolet regimes

In the framework of noncommutative geometry, the encoding of a geometric space by a spectral triple (𝒜,ℋ,D)(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{H},D) reveals information through two complementary spectral regimes of the Dirac operator D:

•The ultraviolet (UV) regime corresponds to the high-energy part of the spectrum, i.e., the behavior of the eigenvalues of DD at infinity. This regime captures the infinitesimal structure of the space and determines its local geometric invariants, such as dimension, volume form, and curvature. In physics, this is akin to probing a system at very short distances or high momenta. Mathematically, the UV behavior governs the asymptotics of the heat kernel and enters crucially in the spectral action principle.

•The infrared (IR) regime concerns the low-lying part of the spectrum of D, particularly the small eigenvalues. This part reflects the global topological and geometric features of the space, such as connectedness, volume growth, and index-theoretic quantities. In physics, IR behavior refers to low-energy phenomena and large-scale properties. It plays a central role in understanding long-range correlations and topological effects.

In particular, such a dual perspective allows noncommutative geometry to access both local spectral invariants and global arithmetic or topological features through a unified operator-theoretic language.
For the infrared regime we construct in [30] self-adjoint operators Dlog(λ,N){D_{\log}^{(\lambda,N)}} obtained as rank-one perturbations of the spectral triple associated with the scaling operator on the interval [λ−1,λ][\lambda^{-1},\lambda] and whose spectrum coincides with the stunning approximation of the low lying zeta zeros as described in the letter to Riemann. We further compute the regularized determinants detreg(Dlog(λ,N)−z)\det\nolimits_{\mathrm{reg}}({D_{\log}^{(\lambda,N)}}-z) of these operators and discuss the analytic role they play in controlling and potentially proving the above result by showing that, suitably normalized, they converge towards the Riemann Ξ\Xi function.
For the ultraviolet regime, we shall briefly describe in Section 7.6 the results of [27] which show that the prolate wave operator provides a self-adjoint operator that matches the ultraviolet behavior of the zeros. As a preparation one can use the explicit formulas to compute the heat expansion, assuming RH, of an operator whose spectrum is formed of the imaginary parts of non-trivial zeros of ζ⁡(z)\zeta(z) :

Theorem 7.3.

where a0=−14a_{0}=-\frac{1}{4} and for k>0k>0, using Bernouilli numbers BjB_{j} and Euler numbers E⁡(k)E(k),

which shows that the asymptotic expansion (30) is by no means convergent since its general coefficient ana_{n} diverges like a factorial.

7.6 The prolate wave operator

The prolate spheroidal wave functions play a key role as we saw above in relation with the Riemann zeta function. In all these applications they appear as eigenfunctions of the angle operator between two orthogonal projections in the Hilbert space L2​(ℝ)ev L^{2}(\mathbb{R})^{\text{ev }} of even square integrable function on ℝ\mathbb{R}. These projections depend on a parameter λ>0\lambda>0, the projection PλP_{\lambda} is given by the multiplication with the characteristic function of the interval [−λ,λ]⊂ℝ[-\lambda,\lambda]\subset\mathbb{R}. The projection Pλ^\widehat{P_{\lambda}} is its conjugate by the Fourier transform 𝔽eℝ\mathbb{F}_{e_{\mathbb{R}}}. In all the above applications of prolate spheroidal wave functions the miraculous existence, discovered by the Bell Labs group of a differential operator P​WλPW_{\lambda} commuting with the angle operator, plays only an auxiliary role. In the present section we explain another "miracle" discovered in our joint work with H. Moscovici [27]: a careful study of the natural self-adjoint extension of P​WλPW_{\lambda} extended to L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) shows that it still has discrete spectrum and that its negative eigenvalues reproduce the ultraviolet behavior of the squares of zeros of the Riemann zeta function. In a similar way the positive spectrum corresponds, in the ultraviolet regime, to the trivial zeros. This coincidence holds for two values λ=1\lambda=1 and λ=2\lambda=\sqrt{2}. The conceptual reason for this coincidence is the link between the operator of (18), i.e.

(PWλψ)(q)=−∂((λ2−q2)∂)ψ(q)+(2πλq)2ψ(q)(\operatorname{PW}_{\lambda}\psi)(q)=\,-\partial((\lambda^{2}-q^{2})\partial)\,\psi(q)+(2\pi\lambda q)^{2}\,\psi(q) (32)

and the square of the scaling operator S̸:=x∂x\not{S}:=x\partial_{x}. As we saw above the compression of the scaling ϑ⁡(f)\vartheta(f) to Sonin’s space was shown to be the root of Weil’s positivity at the archimedean place on test functions with support in the interval [2−1/2,21/2]\left[2^{-1/2},2^{1/2}\right], but I had shown in 1998 that the prolate wave operator admits a unique selfadjoint extension commuting with the orthogonal projections PλP_{\lambda} and Pλ^\widehat{P_{\lambda}}. It is invariant under the Fourier transform and restricts to the Sonin space, i.e. the space of square integrable even functions which vanish identically as well as their Fourier transform on the interval [−λ,λ][-\lambda,\lambda]. We discovered in [27], that this restriction of PWλ\operatorname{PW}_{\lambda} to the Sonin space, which is a selfadjoint operator, provides a spectral realization of the ultraviolet regime of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. More precisely the spectrum of this operator is formed by a discrete sequence νk\nu_{k} of negative numbers and the numbers 2​νk2\sqrt{\nu}_{k} for the choice λ=2\lambda=\sqrt{2} have the same ultraviolet behavior as the ρ−12\rho-\frac{1}{2} where the ρ\rho’s are the zeros of zeta.
In fact using the Darboux process we constructed a Dirac square root DD of PWλ\operatorname{PW}_{\lambda} depending on a deformation parameter, and whose spectrum is formed of the numbers 2​νk2\sqrt{\nu}_{k} for the choice λ=2\lambda=\sqrt{2}, and has the same ultraviolet behavior as the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Figure 2 shows the spectrum of the operator DD and the imaginary parts of zeros of zeta. This ultraviolet spectral similarity suggests that one has spectrally captured the contribution of the archimedean place to the mysterious zeta spectrum. The ambiguity in the choice of the Dirac square root DD is deeply related to the differential Galois theory of the prolate differential equation studied by J. P. Ramis and his collaborators [45, 89].

8 Conclusion

The Riemann Hypothesis has catalyzed the development of vast areas of mathematics, from classical analysis to modern arithmetic geometry and mathematical physics. Each approach has enriched our understanding of the zeta function and its generalizations, even when falling short of a proof.

In this survey, we have provided a comprehensive view of this mathematical landscape. We began with a detailed examination of what is known about the Riemann zeta function and its zeros, then surveyed the remarkable variety of mathematical theories developed over 165 years in pursuit of RH—from classical analytic methods and the theory of L-functions to modern approaches via random matrix theory, operator theory, and arithmetic geometry. We explored equivalent formulations of the hypothesis, each offering its own perspective on why this problem has proven so resistant to solution. While this comprehensive survey demonstrates the richness of mathematical ideas generated by RH, it also reveals how even the most sophisticated modern approaches have yet to crack this 165-year-old puzzle.

Against this backdrop of accumulated knowledge, the second part of this paper offers something different-a return to Riemann’s original viewpoint with fresh eyes. Our discovery of a large class of functions directly related to the Weil quadratic form and with zeros provably on the critical line, combined with the extraordinary numerical evidence linking truncated Euler products to the actual zeros of zeta, suggests that Riemann’s original insights may contain more power than previously realized. The accuracy achieved using only primes less than 13—with errors as small as 2.6×10−552.6\times 10^{-55}—cannot be dismissed as coincidence.

The geometric framework presented here, utilizing the trace formula and spectral methods, offers a potential path forward: proving that zeros of appropriately constructed approximating functions converge to zeros of zeta. This synthesis of computational discovery, classical analysis, and modern geometric techniques represents a new approach that honors Riemann’s legacy while employing contemporary mathematical tools.

Whether this path leads to a proof of RH remains to be seen. However, the journey has already revealed unexpected connections between the Weil quadratic form and the world of information theory, and between computational evidence and theoretical structure. As we wrote in our letter to Riemann, sometimes the most profound truths are hidden in the simplest observations.

For comprehensive surveys of the Riemann Hypothesis and its many facets, see [86, 6, 44, 63, 37, 39]. The present work, to be continued in collaboration with C. Consani and H. Moscovici, offers a new chapter in this ongoing story.
